[Then those great bodhisattvas, headed by Vajragarbha, having again performed worship and prostrated themselves, spoke as follows: (Hodgson manuscript, with slight damage).
Having prostrated in this manner, the Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, Vajragarbha and the others, once again made offerings and, having paid homage, addressed him thus:
"The definitive determination of the meaning of the *tilaka* has been correctly and clearly explained."

Regarding "tilaka": because he is self-arisen within the center of the self (*ātmamadhye*), he is called the Self-Arisen (*svayaṃbhū*). [The reading is *tilake* in manuscript W and *tilake* in manuscript A. [The reading is *madhye* in manuscript A and *madhya* in manuscript W.]
Having become self-arisen, after [the Teacher] had spoken the definitive,
perfectly clear teaching on the meaning of the pure drops (*bindu*) through the drops,
he said:
Because he is self-arisen in the center of myself, he is therefore called "Self-Arisen" (*svayaṃbhū*); for the meaning of *mahābhūta* is that which is to be inferred.

Because it is the object of inference as the true reality; [or, according to W, because it is independent of all that has come into being]. Thus, the Blessed One, the Self-Existent, alone is the presiding deity.
Thus. [Or, according to W, therefore thus.]
The Self-Existent One (*svayaṃbhū*), known as the Great Being who has arisen by himself.
Since he is the object of inference for us,
this self-arisen Blessed One is the sole supreme deity.
"With reference to the deities" refers to the elements previously specified.
"Among them, the most excellent" means in the form of the preeminent one. Regarding the phrase "the supreme deity":
Regarding the "Provinces Spoken of in the Gongdu," it says:
"Because those [provinces] are preeminent in the center,
they are designated by way of their principal forms."
Always abiding in the supreme, delightful secret, which is the self of all.
[Omnipresent] in all selves, O Great Self! How, Blessed One, is there the *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasamvara*?
O Blessed One,
[you who are] all Buddhas,
supremely delighted by the secret!
The self of all abides eternally;
just as the Blessed One is,
so is he in union with all the Buddhas.
Regarding the *Ḍākinīsamvaratantra*: otherwise, how and by what means is the supreme, most beneficial vow [attained]?
How and by what means? [How] by this?
The secret of the secondary [meaning] and the secret of words are proclaimed as the quality (*guṇa*).
The secret of words;
[the word] *guṇa* is present in A, while it is omitted in W;
"Otherwise, in this manner..."
From the *Extremely Beneficial for the Dompa*:
"The secret term refers to that which possesses qualities; the secret is likewise renowned as a quality."
The term "Vajrin" is figurative; it is to be abandoned as it is censured in the supreme and beautiful worldly [tradition].
"The secret of words" is a form of Mlecchita (corrupt speech).
This object of knowledge is indeed perceptible and follows from external [evidence];
the Vajra-holder possesses qualities,
having abandoned the contempt of the world’s supreme ones.
The secret language is the speech of the barbarians;
even by seeking it externally,
this should be known through direct perception.
When the mind is not perceived through the term "inferential" (*anumāna-gauṇya*),
it is called "mind" (*citta*) as the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) and the qualities themselves (*guṇa*).
By means of the words of the virtuous one, Rjes dpag yon tan can,
when the mind is not seen, even that which is called "mind" [is not seen].
Possessing qualities and proclaiming qualities,
he always abides within the supreme, delightful secret, the self of all;
the secret is his very being, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The secret state: established there in the Self of all, in every possible way.
In the supreme secret joy,
he dwells eternally as the self of all.
In this secret, the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) abides; therein,
the self-nature of all things resides, and therein,
all things are fully established.
Who is this "Vajrin of Emptiness" who rejoices together with bliss?
[The text reads: *śūnyavajrī* (O Vajrin of Emptiness);
[he] rejoices together with bliss (*saham ānandeti*).
When the form of the mind, consisting of colors such as blue and so forth, is not seen,
and when the ears and other senses do not hear, what kind of mind is there then? How, in that case, could there be an inference of it?
The form of the mind;
they are heard by the ear and the other [senses].
It is heard [in the scriptures].
As for the one who possesses the vajra of emptiness:
It is joyful together with suffering; when the form of the mind is not seen by the eyes as blue or otherwise,
[it is joyful].
When sounds and so forth are not heard,
at that time, what is the mind like?
At that time, how does inference function?
And nothing else is seen by the sense of smell; what fragrance could there be in two things that are impure?
And the mind is not seen externally;
nor is it [found] through external enjoyments, such as sweet or bitter tastes.
Nor by enjoyments, nor by mental applications,
and likewise not from tactile sensations.
If this is not perceived by the nose,
does the sweet fragrance abide in the center?
The mind is not perceived externally, nor is there such proximate sensory enjoyment; its taste is neither sweet nor bitter.
Likewise, as for the tangible itself:
"He who always abides in the secret, supreme, and delightful state, which is the self of all—
such as he is in the secret, they meditate upon through inference."
In the secret [teaching],
this: "In the supreme joy of the secret,
he who is the self of all dwells eternally."
"How is this secret to be conceived through inference?
It is like knowledge that has entered into written letters."
[The Blessed One said: "O Blessed One, apart from written letters, what kind of sound would be a deity? What would it be like?"
What kind of sound? What kind of word? What kind of deity? As for the form of the letters:
Is it the very gnosis of the Perfection [of Wisdom] itself?
Or else, O Blessed One, how is it that you speak thus?
And how is it that you are called "Deva"?
O All-Buddhas, for what purpose indeed is there a union (*samāyoga*), and what is it called?
From what is the *ḍākinī* designated? What indeed is the *jāla* (net)? From what designation is the *jāla* indeed [derived]?
What is the definitive meaning of all the Buddhas?
What is meant by "equal union"? And what is the name of the ḍākinī?
What is meant by "restraint" (*saṃvara*), and likewise, what is meant by "those who act wickedly" (*duścāriṇyaḥ*)?

"Is it not passion (*rāga*) that you have spoken of, nor likewise dispassion (*virāga*), nor anything else? To whom does the designation 'the Middle Way' belong, and how can there be the illusion of all women?"
What is explained by the term *saṃjñā*? It is all women through illusion (*māyā*); thus it is called *Sdom pa* (Saṃvara).
Likewise, it is difficult to practice;
why do you say there is no passion? And likewise for that which is not free from passion.
What is that which is called "Madhyamaka"?
What is the illusion of all women?
Are emptiness, form, the element, and so forth explained [as such]? What is the purpose of their equality?
And likewise, the cloth-painting of the universal lotus (*viśvapadmapaṭa*) is of six kinds, as previously described; [it consists of] the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth,
which are [characterized by] emptiness.
Whatever is explained, one should apply it to equanimity; first,
there are the six transformations,
and the images drawn upon variegated lotuses.
The great seal (mahāmudrā) of the vowels and consonants, as well as the yoga of those whose intention is not directed toward reality— what would constitute the true reality?
Explain the external seal and the yoga of meditative absorption.
And likewise,
that which is concentrated,
the great mudrā of *Āli* and *Kali*.
What is the yoga of the mind that lacks suchness,
and how does the excellence of suchness come to be?
What is meditative equipoise within yoga itself?
The external is also explained as pure:
what would be the rising of the suns and moons of the Perfect Buddhas?
What kind [of it] should it be? How should the mandala be established after having drawn the drawing upon the ground?
[Regarding the phrase *lekhatvālekhyaṃ*: W reads *lekhyavā alekhyaṃ*; A reads *lekhatvālekhyaṃ*. "The Sun of Perfectly Complete Awakening has been written; what kind of arising is it?"
How should the maṇḍala be arranged, both the one that is drawn and the one that is not drawn? And likewise for the mantra-tantra as well.
I do not know the secret seat (*guhyapīṭha*), especially the four lotuses (*catuṣpadma*).
One should not seek the secret place;
rather, the four lotuses are especially distinguished.
What is the self? The self [is] consciousness, and likewise, consciousness is non-consciousness.

How is it that consciousness (*vijñāna*) has the nature of consciousness (*cit*), and likewise, how is it that the self (*ātman*) and non-self (*anātman*) are both consciousness (*citta*) and non-consciousness (*acitta*)?
How is it that knowledge (*jñāna*) has the nature of consciousness (*cit*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is exactly the same?
How are "self" and "mine"?
Likewise,
what are "mind" and "mental factors" themselves?
It is said that the nature of the mind is primordial wisdom (*jñāna*); likewise, consciousness itself [is it]. So too are the relationship of cause and effect, as well as virtue and non-virtue.

What is declared to be the stream of a river, and especially the ocean? What is the cause and effect [of these]? What are dharma and adharma? What is called the flow of a river, and what specifically is the ocean?
The stream [is] proclaimed as the entity of cause and effect.
In the same way, what is said regarding the stream of a river and its nature as a phenomenon?
Even the ocean is likewise distinguished.
You have taught manifoldness; why then is multiplicity not perceived?
[To this question, the answer refers to the Śaivasiddhānta.]
You have taught the knowledge of consciousness and so forth, as well as the elixir of life (*rasāyana*);
yet how is it that many do not attain these very things?
O Vidyārāja, you have spoken of consciousness and primordial wisdom;
likewise, you have explained the extraction of essences, as well as the *ālīḍha* and other postures, and furthermore, the mastery of the bow.
Is it a secondary or primary meaning of the word? For what indeed has been spoken even by the Kalpa? What [is the case]? Is it the word? Or the sound?
[The reading *gauṇyā* is supported by W; *gaunyā* by A. [The reading *mukhyam* is supported by A; *myukhyam* by W. [The particle *hi* is present in W; it is omitted in A.]
What is the meaning of "stretching out the left leg" and so forth?
What is the meaning of "victory by means of the bow" and likewise the others?
And what is the meaning of the terms "primary" and "non-primary"?
What was said regarding "investigation" (*vīkṣaṇa*)?
The thirty-seven great factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), as well as the internal body and so forth.
The Śrāvaka vehicle has been taught by you; what is the purpose of that as well?
The dharmas of great enlightenment consist of thirty-seven internal factors,
as well as others such as the [three] bodies (kāya) and so forth.
"What is the purpose for which the Śrāvakas speak of you?
What need is there for that? By what cause or connection is Vajrasattva Great Bliss?
[He is] blissful.

Hari was likewise [there],
as was Kāmadeva, and the beautiful Umādevī, his own wife. [She was there] together with her husband.

The goddess who averts hardship, of beautiful form:

Having gone for refuge to the Guru,

I am the Buddha, I am Vajrasattva, I am Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hari, and Śaśin; I am Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu; Hari;

"If the Vajradhara is thus peaceful,

What is the Saṃbhogakāya?

How did he become the form of Yama, and likewise the supreme steed?
As He-ru-ka spoke,

In the same way, the supreme horse itself is thus described as being of various kinds for the gentle deities,
the goddesses, and likewise for the wrathful ones.
Whatever various things you have spoken in a barbarian tongue— even by that,

First of all, has the speech of the Goddess been extracted from the *Devatīmāyāvāda* by the practitioners of mantra?

The *samavasaraṇa* is the abode of Śrī Vajrasattva, joined with the wisdom-mudrās and the Vajra goddesses.

The term "secret" (*gsang ba*) refers to the sevenfold aspect; thus, it means "the seventh. The eighth is the characteristic of the ineffable. By the term "secret," the non-duality of mind and mental factors is spoken of as the Tathāgata himself. Because they are of one taste in suchness and of one essence, they arise as secret; therefore, it is "secret. To pervade all space is the measure of the Bhagavān. The Blessed One said:

The Blessed One said: "In that which is supremely excellent, within the sphere of supreme gnosis; delightful, charming, and devoid of all comparison—delightful because it is charming through the act of sporting in union with Locanā and the others."

[delightful] \A, [omitted] \W;

"Delightful" (*ramya*) means preeminent and sublime; it is the object of supreme gnosis (*jñāna*). "In delight" (*ramamāṇe*) means while experiencing joy, which is free from all metaphors. It is "in delight" because one experiences joy through the perfect union with the eyes and so forth.
The union with Śrī Vajrasattva through the assemblies of all goddesses.
All goddesses, extending to the limits of the realm of space, are great bliss.
Endowed with the bliss of all yogas, they are sinless and prevail by their own power;
being endowed with bliss, they apply themselves [to it].
"Possessed of supreme happiness" (*sukhottama*) [is the reading in W]; "endowed with pleasure" (*sukhānvita*) [is the reading in A].
It is delightful because they take pleasure in the *puruṣāyita* (man-like) positions, gladdening one another.
"It is delightful because of the acts of a man" is the conjectured reading; the manuscripts A and W read "It is delightful because of the acts of a woman (*rūpāyitaiḥ*).
This corresponds to *SBS* 3.13cd.

Through this union with the glorious Vajrasattva and through proceeding in equality with all goddesses, reaching to the very limits of the expanse of space, one possesses the bliss of all unions—the great bliss of all goddesses. The power arising from this is immeasurable; through mutual delight, they bring joy, and the pleasure of those persons and their consorts is that of intense rapture.

The self of all is the universal self (*sarvātmā*). Thus, O sons of noble family, that which was previously called the "abode of the Blessed One" is so designated because it is considered to consist of the essence of all Tathāgatas; it is called such by virtue of being the universal self. By the phrase "in this way, as the universal self," the perfection of the place is described.
(Note: *pūrvam uktam* is corrected from *pūrvam uktāṃ*; *yasmāt* is corrected from *tasmāt*.)
[The reading] *°ātmakaṃ matam* is found in A; [the reading] *°ātmakagataḥ* is found in W. [The reading] *evaṃbhūtena* is found in A; [the reading] *evaṃbhūte* is found in W.
[The reading] *uktā* is found in W; [the reading] *uktam* is found in A.

"Everything is the self" means that it is the self of all. O son of noble family, it is in this way that the Blessed One previously spoke of the abode. Therefore, he spoke of the Tathāgatas as being the self of all, and by means of "everything being the self," he spoke of that perfect abundance of the abode.
Thus, in the manner described, [it is established] through the nature of the present state in the abode.
It is said that he always remains within the inner apartments, because [he exists] by way of his own intrinsic nature (*svābhāvataḥ*).

"However many there may be" refers to the fact that, by their very nature as having been individually generated in the state described, they always abide in the midst of a retinue of consorts; thus it is said. And all those Buddhas—meaning all the Buddhas—are equal in number to the atoms within all world-systems. Because they have been fashioned by the Tathāgatas as being eternal and so forth, or because they have that as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are called "consisting of all Buddhas" (*sarvabuddhamaya*). The suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in the sense of cause (*hetu*) or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because they have that as their intrinsic nature, it is said by the Tathāgatas— or perhaps simply "it is said"— that [they are such].

This Buddha is all Buddhas, equal in number to the atoms of all world-systems. Because he was created by the Tathāgatas, such as the Permanent One (*nitya*), or because of his essential nature (*svabhāva*), the locus is called "the reality of all Buddhas" (*sarvabuddhatattva*); that is, it is the reality (*vastu*) in terms of cause or essential nature. Because he is devoted to the welfare of sentient beings (*sattvārtha*), he is a *sattva*. Because he cannot be moved by any conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and because his intrinsic nature is wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya-jñāna-svabhāva*), he is Vajrasattva.

"Union" (*samāyoga*) means "conjunction. Where does it occur? It occurs in the secret place; for [the consort] is the very nature of the source of all phenomena (*dharmodaya*), and not otherwise. Furthermore, by means of the nine limbs, such as the emanation through his own pure essence, he completely embraces her—from every aspect—as being of that same nature, like water merging with milk, by means of his single body which possesses the perfection of enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*).

Then, through the yoga of the great maṇḍala, having realized and understood the reality of all external and internal phenomena, and having correctly performed [this] in a single instant, they—along with that *sarvabuddha* (all-buddha) together with those others—possess the perfect union (*samyak yoga*) with all the Buddhas. This "union with all the Buddhas" (*sarvabuddhasamāyoga*) occurs simultaneously, not at different times, but at once; because all [beings] have become one through that meditative absorption of mind-only (*cittamātra-samāpatti*), and because of the state of being all-pervasive through mutual passion and the nature of all things, it is called the "union with all the Buddhas. *Rāgaṇa* (Note: The term *rāgaṇa* appears in the manuscript fragment provided).

Then, through the yoga of the great maṇḍala, one realizes and knows in a single instant that very [reality] within all external and internal entities, just as it was performed by all the Buddhas. Therefore, the "perfect union with all the Buddhas and others" is the union with equality (*samatā-yoga*). The time of equality is the time of non-differentiation; because, by means of the state of union, one enters into equanimity as mere mind through all [entities], they are gathered together into a single entity. Since this proceeds as the nature of all entities, it is called "union with equality with all the Buddhas."

One’s own and their forms are "one's own forms"; the complete transformation of those—the ālayavijñāna, the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and so forth—is the complete transformation of one’s own essence. By meditating on the samādhi of selflessness, one abides in the nature of the mirror-like, the equality, the discerning, and the all-accomplishing [wisdoms], and thereby becomes irreversible; this is the meaning. Because the nature of illusion of all women is the siddhi through the complete transformation of one’s own essence, it is said: "By the joy of bestowing happiness upon all who obtain her, all women will be accomplished."

"Vicitrā" (variegated) and "māyā" (illusion) constitute "vicitramāyā. It consists of various colors and forms, having the appearance of all goddesses and so forth; that is her "vicitramāyā. Having established this in the mind by means of the apprehension "this is the mudrā," he says "Ḍākinī. The meaning is that she is the "vicitramāyāmudrā" because she moves through the sky in the ten directions while the Blessed One Vajrasattva is situated in the midst of his inner circle.
The departure into the sky of one who was situated in the midst of his own inner apartments.

"Various and illusory" means that they possess the forms of all goddesses and so forth, arising from various colors and shapes. Having grasped this mudrā of various illusions and established it in the mind, he spoke these words: "O Ḍākinī, the space of the ten directions that has entered into the midst of the retinue of the consorts of the Blessed Lord Vajrasattva himself—this very movement is the meaning of what is called the 'mudrā of various illusions.'"

The meaning is that it is a manifest speech, established by its own convention and well-known through all mundane and supramundane treatises. By such designations as "ḍākinī" and so forth, the deity is being described. This is because all women are the Blessed One’s Vajra Goddesses. They are perfected for him through the transformation (*parāvṛtti*) of the eightfold basis—beginning with the *ālayavijñāna* of saṃsāra—characterized by the mirror-like, equality, discerning, and all-accomplishing gnoses, and by their nature as illusion. Having the diverse illusory forms of the mirror-like gnosis and the others, their activity of traveling through space by means of illusion becomes like a manifold form. Therefore, this "seal of manifold illusion" (*vicitramāyāmudrā*) is designated as "ḍākinī."

This means that it is composed by oneself using an unintelligible language, which is renowned within all the treatises of both the mundane and the supramundane. These [deities] such as the ḍākinīs are taught here in brief. Because all women are the Vajra Goddesses of the Blessed One, they are established as having the nature of various illusions—the mirror-like, the equality, the discriminating, and the all-accomplishing wisdoms—which are achieved through the characteristic of turning back from abiding in the eight [consciousnesses], such as the *ālayavijñāna* that functions as cyclic existence. Since their own essence consists of the various illusions of those [wisdoms], such as the mirror-like wisdom, the activity of moving through space via those illusions results in various forms; therefore, this mudrā of various illusions is to be called "ḍākinī."

The ability to travel through space belonging not only to those *mlecchas* is called *ḍākinī*; thus, the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of moving everywhere in space is established as *ḍākinī*. Therefore, he concludes with the word "from all" (*sarvataḥ*). The "universal seals" (*viśvamudrāḥ*) are the various seals (*mudrāḥ*) in the ten directions, namely the seals of Locanā and the others. By means of the yoga of reflection, one seals the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*); therefore, they are called "seals. Alternatively, the "universal seals" are all the seals of the glorious Vajrasattva, who is the universal being (*viśva*) or the totality of phenomena (*sarvabhāva*).
And all [the reflections];

and all sounds.

It is not that the activity of a single ḍākinī who moves through the sky of the *kḷa klos de* is what is referred to as "ḍākinī"; rather, it is explained thus: "She who accomplishes the universal movement in space is renowned as the Ḍākinī. Regarding the term "from all" (*kun las*), it refers to the ten directions. "Various" (*sna tshogs*) and its "mudrās" (*phyag rgya*) refer to the various mudrās, such as those of Locanā and the others. Because one seals the realm of sentient beings through the yoga of the reflected image (*bimba-yoga*), they are called "mudrās. "Various" (*sna tshogs*) means the nature of all, or Śrī-Vajrasattva and all [deities]; and their "mudrās" are the various mudrās.

The *ḍākinī* is one whose form is the movement through all space, [endowed] with all kinds of blisses through all types of universal vows (*viśvasamvara*). Regarding the term "Buddha-element" (*buddhadhātu*): the elements (*dhātavaḥ*) that constitute the nature of the manifestation of the basis of the Buddha Śrī Vairocana, as well as the elements that are the nature of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, are designated by the word "Buddha-element. Just as the elements that are the causes for the manifestation of the basis of Śrī Vajrasattva and those elements that possess his nature are indicated by the word *ḍākinī*—having the nature of moving through space—in the same way, the elements of Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Amogha are to be understood.
Vairocana, Akṣobhya, and Ratneśa...

Regarding the phrase "the various types of *saṃvara*," this refers to the manifold forms; the *ḍākinī* is the essence that pervades all space through supreme bliss. The term "Buddha-sphere" (*buddha-garbha*) refers to the causal factors for the manifestation [of enlightenment] while abiding in the Buddha Śrī Vairocana; these are his own constituent elements (*dhātu*). The spheres that are the nature of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas are expressed by the word "Buddha-sphere. Just as the causal factors for the manifestation [of enlightenment] while abiding in the glorious Vajrasattva are the constituent elements of his own nature, the term *ḍākinī* is taught as having the nature of moving through space. In the same way, the spheres of Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi are to be understood.

"Regarding *sarvabuddhaḍākinī*: when the Blessed One Vajrasattva is surrounded by Locanā and the others, his movement through the sky is the *ḍākinī* whose self-nature is all Vajrasattvas. Likewise, when Śrī Heruka is surrounded by Gaurī and the others, his movement through the sky is the *ḍākinī* whose self-nature is all Herukas. Similarly, for one engaged in the yoga of Nairātmyā, when [the deities] such as Vajrā have passed into parinirvāṇa, their movement through the sky is the *ḍākinī* whose self-nature is all Nairātmyās. Likewise, for one endowed with gnosis (*jñāna*), when [the deities] such as Vajraḍākinī have passed into parinirvāṇa, their movement through the sky is called the *ḍākinī* whose self-nature is the gnosis of all gnoses. In the same way, [one may visualize] Padminī together with Tārā, or Yama with Yamacakrā, or likewise Paramāśva and Trailokyavijaya. Or else, whatever else is desired by the mind, differentiated according to the divisions of the families, should be visualized in the same manner, surrounded by ḍākinīs."

It is said.

Regarding the phrase "the ḍākinīs of all Buddhas": this refers to all those who traverse the sky surrounding the Blessed Lord Vajrasattva with [his consorts] Locanā and the others, being ḍākinīs whose very nature is that of Vajrasattva; likewise, all those who traverse the sky surrounding Śrī Heruka with [his consorts] Pāṇḍarā and the others, being ḍākinīs whose very nature is that of Heruka; likewise, all those who traverse the sky surrounding Nairātmyā with [her consorts] Vajrā and the others, being ḍākinīs whose very nature is that of Nairātmyā; likewise, all those who traverse the sky surrounding the Wisdom-Endowed One (Jñānavat) with Vajraḍākinī and the others, being ḍākinīs whose very nature is Wisdom; and similarly, Tārā together with Padmāvatī, Padmacakra, Yamāntaka, as well as Paramāśva, and likewise Trailokyavijaya himself—furthermore, whatever is desired by the mind is also described as being surrounded by ḍākinīs distinguished by their respective clan divisions.

Having thus indicated the *Ḍākinī* who is the essence of all Buddhas, he explains the *saṃvara*: "Bliss" refers to that ultimate bliss which arises through the union (*samāyoga*) with the Lord Śrīvajrasattva’s own gnosis-mudrā. What is that? It is the "excellent" (*vara*), the supreme, because it is the most preeminent of all forms of bliss; it is attained through that very application of *māyā* and not by any other, meaning not through the yoga of any of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

Thus, having revealed the ḍākinīs of all the Buddhas, in order to explain the *saṃvara* (vow), it says "Bliss": that which, through union with the wisdom-mudrā of the Blessed One, the glorious Vajrasattva, generates one who possesses supreme bliss. What happens from that? It is "supreme," meaning exceptionally exalted, because it is the preeminent means for all bliss. For that very reason, it is the "application of all illusions"; furthermore, this means that it is not like the union of others, such as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Because that very bliss which arises through the applications of the *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga* and the *Ḍākinījāla* is expressed by the word "saṃ" (bliss), for that reason that bliss arises as the most excellent and supreme. The parinirvāṇa of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas [is surpassed by] the arising of great compassion through the awakening to all phenomena as being like an illusion, which constitutes its purification.

Because it generates bliss precisely through the application of the *ḍākinījāla* (the web of ḍākinīs) that is equal to all Buddhas, it is designated by the term *sām*. Therefore, when one realizes all phenomena—which are like an illusion and are the purification of the parinirvāṇa of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—as being the cause that generates that supreme and distinguished bliss, great compassion arises.

The statement that "the triple world is not empty" is because of the existence of unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), and because within that unreal imagination, emptiness exists. Nor is it "not non-empty," because from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the conceptualization of grasped object and grasping subject is absent. Furthermore, even that cognition by which the absence of grasped object and grasping subject is directly realized is not perceived, since it lies beyond the range of conceptualization. Therefore, such cognition is the meaning of the "middle way. And [there is] unreal imagination...

"Neither empty" means that because the three realms and the objects of false conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*) regarding the conduct of desire are entities, they are empty as false conceptualizations; thus, they are "entities. "Nor non-empty" means that in the ultimate sense, the entities of the conceptualization of subject and object do not exist. Through whatever wisdom one directly realizes the non-existence of the entities of subject and object, that wisdom itself does not become an object of observation, because it is not within the domain of conceptualization. For this very reason, the meaning is that one should realize the Middle Way through authentic wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*).

And that is called the yoga of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-yoga*); it is itself the means (*upāya*) because it is conjoined with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). For the Blessed Buddhas, whose nature consists of the object of focus and who are of the essence of compassion, there is therefore "the means of excellent compassion" (*sukaruṇopāya*). Excellent compassion is [great compassion]; in relation to excellent compassion, non-objectified compassion is great compassion. That very thing which has this as its means is "the means of excellent compassion. The connection is: "What kind of one, being of the nature of non-abiding nirvāṇa, became the glorious Vairocana, the speech of Dharma? [Note: *sukaruṇāpekṣayā* is corrected from *sukaruṇāpekṣāyā*.]

It is said: "The union with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-yoga*)," which refers to the very method (*upāya*), because it is endowed with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). The objective focus (*ālambana*) of the Blessed Buddha’s nature of compassion is the essence of compassion itself. Therefore, "the beautiful method of compassion" means that compassion is both beautiful and the method; it is great compassion that does not take an objective focus through equanimity (*upekṣā*). That itself is the method. This method, which is endowed with supreme compassion, is the nature of non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*), namely, the glorious Vairocana. How does this come about? It is to be connected with the phrase: "the phenomena have arisen."

How is it that one "clearly conceptualizes" the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)? Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the discernment of phenomena in the manner of an illusion; that very [wisdom], having gone beyond (*ita*) one's own meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), is the perfection of wisdom. It is not that the perfection of wisdom is clearly manifest. By what means? Through non-conceptual resolute conviction (*avikalpādhimokṣa*). What does one do while conceptualizing? The sense is: by the power of previous sovereign influence (*pūrvādhipatya*).

How is one correctly engaged with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)? That which is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*) should be analyzed as the thorough discernment of phenomena as being like an illusion; that itself is my own excellence. That which is called "perfection" (*pāramitā*) indicates having gone to the further shore; it is said, "the clarity of the perfection of wisdom. By what means? It is by means of non-conceptual resolute belief (*adhimukti*). What does it do? It intends that "that which is analyzed" [is accomplished] through the power of the master.

What is he conceptualizing? He is conceptualizing the nature of all conceptualizations as being like an independent illusion, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth. Regarding what kind of phenomena? Regarding non-conceptual phenomena. What is the conceptualization of the welfare of sentient beings? It is conceptualization by the power of compassion; for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, there is the conceptualization of the welfare of sentient beings. Of what nature is this conceptualization? It is equal to the sound of an echo (*pratiśrutkā-rava-samā*). An "echo" (*pratiśrutkā*) is a reflected sound. That which has a sound equal to that echo—the sound that follows it—is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), whose nature consists of the conceptualization of sound. This [conceptualization] is equal to the sound of an echo. Conceptualizing in this way, he then became the Speech of Dharma (*dharmavāc*). Therefore, from that, he is Vairocana and the others, whose form consists of the conceptualization of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of phenomena, meaning, purpose, etymological explanation, and eloquence. "Speech of Dharma" means the speech that illuminates the three samayas, the sound. Such speech exists, and thus he is called by that name.

Regarding the phrase "examined by all examinations" (*parīkṣita*): "all examinations" refers to the nature of forms and so forth, which are like illusions and lack independent existence. Regarding the phrase "from the characteristics": "the purpose of sentient beings is thoroughly examined in relation to non-conceptual phenomena" means that, through the power of compassion, one examines the causes for the welfare of sentient beings. If one asks what results from such examination, it is said: "equality like an echo. An "echo" refers to the sound of an echo in a mountain cave. Through that, one follows the melody equally and with total equality; and because the nature of sound is conceptual, through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), it is equal like an echo, and having become thus, it is examined. Why is this? Because of the statement: "From this, the speech of the Dharma arises. Therefore, from that [wisdom], the definitive words of the meaning of the Dharma appear individually; this individual cognition is the nature of examination. For that very reason, this clarifies the three pledges (*samaya*) of the glorious Vairocana and the others. "The Dharma of speech" has the meaning of the melody of speech. Having become thus, it is the articulation of speech; this speech is expressed in that very way.

"Then it was accomplished"—this is because of the accomplishment of the Dharma-speech. That Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) is the Bodhisattva path which possesses fruit, established through the *sūtras* such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* by virtue of its sevenfold greatness. Even more excellent than that is the Vajrayāna, because it accomplishes Buddhahood and so forth in this very life. Its truly existent qualities are the powers (*bala*), the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), and so on; their extensive continuity constitutes the "extensive truly existent qualities. By means of these extensive truly existent qualities, all the Tathāgatas—Vairocana and the others—who belong to the three times (past, future, and present) and possess the three samayas, whose nature is body, speech, and mind, are praised. How? All the Tathāgatas praise [them] through non-conceptual resolute conviction (*avikalpādhimokṣa*), according to the principle of a reflected image and so forth.
Vairocana and the others indeed came into being.

That which is established from what is not incorrect is established through the *dharmakāya* (the body of reality). That vehicle and that greatness is the "Great Vehicle" (*Mahāyāna*), namely the path of the bodhisattvas together with its fruit. It is established in the sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* by way of being applied to the seven types of greatness. Therefore, the Vajrayāna—the Great Vehicle that is supremely distinguished—is for the sake of thoroughly accomplishing the Buddha and so forth in this very life. Its supreme qualities are the powers, fearlessnesses, and so on; their "collection" is extensive because those qualities are supreme. The "three times" are the past, the future, and the present. The "three samayas" refer to all things whose nature is body, speech, and mind. "All Tathāgatas" refers to Vairocana and the others. As for the manner of praise: they are praised by all the Tathāgatas through the knowledge of reflected images and so forth, by means of liberation free from conceptual construction.

Because all things, whether stable or moving, are pervaded by the nature of emptiness, and because the three realms of existence—which consist of mere representation—are pervaded by that [emptiness], it is therefore taught that the yoga of the deity resides within the stable and moving worlds.

Because the nature of emptiness pervades all things without exception—whether stable or moving—and because the three realms are merely consciousness pervaded by that [emptiness] such as stability and movement, the yoga of the deity is taught for the sake of the vows and so forth.
[Objection: O Blessed One, if everything has that very nature, why does the world not perceive it in that form?

"Bhagavān, why is it that its nature is not perceived by the world in all its aspects? The Bhagavān replied: "Because—for this reason—in every way and in every respect, [the world] does not perceive itself; that is, it does not perceive the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), the sixfold body of consciousness, which is based upon itself. Because of their own self-awareness in the form of mind (*citta*), the deluded—those confused persons such as the Naiyāyikas and others—do not understand it; due to their bewilderment, they do not know it."

The Blessed One said: "For what reason" is the logical justification (*hetu*). "All-self" means by way of the entity of all things. "Of the self" means one's own. "In the aggregate of consciousness" refers to that which is within the body of consciousness. "Abiding" is the nature of the mind as self-reflexive awareness; therefore, "delusion" is ignorance (*moha*). "Base persons" refers to the followers of the Nyāya school and others. "Unable to comprehend" means they do not know because they are possessed by delusion.

If, O Blessed One, they do not know [this], how could there be an understanding of reality? To this he says: "Cetā" means one whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*); "citta" refers to the sentient being whose nature is consciousness, which everywhere consists of the experience of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, whether auspicious or inauspicious; it is the *jīva*. "Consisting of knowledge" (*jñānamaya*) means the *puruṣa* who consists of all-pervading consciousness. Regarding "the nature of the object of knowledge" (*jñeyasvarūpa*), the proponents of Īśvara hold that the cause of phenomena (*dharma*) is Īśvara alone. In the Śaiva Siddhānta, the "possessor of qualities" (*dharmī*) is Maheśvara, who is accepted by the Māheśvaras as being of the nature of merit (*puṇya*) and so forth, and as the source of the operation of these qualities. To demonstrate this, he has stated positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). He provides the reason (*hetu*) and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the two properties of plurality and unity, which are the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). By the words "of the qualities" (*dharmāṇām*) and so forth, if plurality is stated as the reason for the probandum, then multiplicity would not be established.
In the Śaivasiddhānta, the reason has been stated.

"Bhagavān, if that [Self] does not act, how is it that its reality acts? The Buddha replied: "That which is called 'mind, mental factors, and the nature of mind' is the essence of the minds of sentient beings. 'Mind' refers to the vital activity (*jīva*) whose nature is to cognize all things, such as the aggregates of virtuous entities and so forth. That which is called 'the nature of primordial wisdom' (*jñāna*) is omnipresent; therein, the Person (*puruṣa*) is the nature of the all-pervading primordial wisdom. That which is called 'having the nature of the knowable' refers to the male (*śeṣa*), the one born from the male (*śeṣaja*), the feeler (*vedaka*), the agent (*kartṛ*), the sense of location, the possessor of its own essence, and the state of being an agent. Those who propound Īśvara say that Īśvara is the agent of phenomena. Regarding the phrase 'that very entity which possesses qualities' (*dharmī*): according to the Siddhānta, they assert that the Great Īśvara is the agent of qualities such as merit and so forth, or that he is the nature of those qualities. To demonstrate this, he taught positive and negative concomitance, as well as the one and the many, the probandum (*sādhya*), the subjects (*dharmin*), the logical reasons (*hetu*), and the examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). In the passage beginning with 'of phenomena,' and regarding the word 'many': if 'manyness' itself were stated as the reason for establishing the probandum, then manyness would not produce [the result], because it is not produced."

By this, the proof for identity has been stated; furthermore, both the river and the ocean are intended as the examples. By this, an example must be stated for the sake of proving both multiplicity and unity. Regarding multiplicity first: the plurality—that is, the state of being many—of the phenomena (dharmas) just mentioned, such as consciousness and so forth, which exists by way of exclusion from the one through a manifold continuity, serves as the reason. Thus, for the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), consciousness and the other phenomena appear in many forms.

By stating this in order to establish oneness alone, the examples of both the river and the ocean are also expressed. This should be illustrated by means of the one and the many: first, regarding the many properties, that which is expressed as the culmination of the many entities such as the mind is "multiplicity" (*bahutva*). For this reason, the phrase "by means of the many properties" refers to the various forms of the non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) mind and so forth, which are held to be manifold.
"Is anything apprehended, Blessed One? he asked.
“Blessed One, is it an object?

He replied: “By the term ‘the flow of a river’ (*nadīsrotas*), [it is meant that] just as outside the great ocean the flow of rivers—the movement of water-currents such as the Śītā, Sindhu, Gaṅgā, and so forth—is perceived as distinct, such that one thinks, ‘This is the water of the Śītā, this is the water of the Sindhu, this is the water of the Gaṅgā,’ so too, for the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) who exist outside the profound and bottomless *dharmadhātu*, there appears a variety of things, such as ‘self’ (*ātman*), ‘life-principle’ (*jīva*), ‘person’ (*puruṣa*), and ‘individual’ (*pudgala*).”
This water appears as manifold;
[it is] for those who are externalized.

By the phrase "the flow of rivers," the Śrāvakas are indicated. "The ocean" refers to that which lies beyond the small seas; for example, the continuous flow of rivers such as the Śītā, the Sindhu, and the Gaṅgā, which circulates extensively, is designated as "the river Sindhu" or "the river Gaṅgā"—it is not perceived as having various distinct identities. Likewise, from the profound and unfathomable dharmadhātu, the various entities such as the *ātman*, *puruṣa*, *pudgala*, and *jīva* of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), who stand outside [of it], are likewise [not perceived as distinct].
"Bhagavān, is it that reality here consists of many different types?"

"No," he says. "Reality is one. That reality which is intended here must be grasped as having a single form. Why? Because of such statements as "oneness and multiplicity" and so forth. Regarding "multiplicity": that multiplicity of those things, such as consciousness (*ceta*) and the rest—that is, their existence in various modes—is not perceived; it is not established by reasoning. This is because its existence in multiplicity [is subsumed] within oneness. Just as the multiplicity of rivers exists within the ocean, so too do consciousness, the self, and so forth exist. It is not understood through reasoning; even when consciousness and the rest, though existing, enter into the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), their diversity does not appear. Just as there is an absence of the appearance of plurality for rivers established in the oceans, so too, due to the absence of multiplicity, reality should be understood as having a single form alone.
Likewise, because of the absence of multiplicity.

It is not that [the Buddha] has spoken [this] arbitrarily; rather, whatever is asserted here as being truly one, it is precisely that which is taught as having the nature of that very reality (*tattva*). For, regarding the expressions "one" and "many," what is called "manyness" refers to those things such as the mind (*citta*) and so forth, which are manifold and diverse in form. These are not objects of observation for the Noble Ones (*ārya*), nor are they realized through reasoning. Because manyness enters into the one—just as, for example, the manyness of rivers enters into the great ocean—one does not realize through reasoning that the mind, the self (*ātman*), and so forth exist. Even though there is reasoning [that supports their existence], when the mind and so forth enter into the selflessness (*anātman*) of all phenomena, at that time their diversity is no longer asserted. For example, when many rivers enter the great ocean, there is no longer any appearance of distinct entities. Likewise, because the entity of manyness does not exist, reality is realized solely in its aspect of oneness.

From where is such a reality obtained? It is obtained from the mouth of the Guru, for the Guru is the one who instructs in the *mantras* and *tantras*; that which is obtained through his words and instructions is what he now points out in this instruction. Regarding "the internal" (*adhyātma*), he asks: in what manner are those very channels (*nāḍī*) and subtle apertures (*suśira*) established, and where are they situated? He says: "The secret seat (*guhyapīṭha*) is adorned with the five voids. In the region of the lotus’s pericarp (*varaṭaka*), within the subtle apertures of the channels, there is that which flows as blood, urine, and semen, and which seizes the semen. This is located in the space of the five channel-apertures; or rather, it is characterized by the qualities of water, fire, Indra (earth), wind, cold, heat, both, and extreme heat. It is adorned by these five voids situated within the circle of passion (*rāgamaṇḍala*). He says that it is not adorned by the five voids alone, but is also embellished by the lotus.
