“With affection” (*sānurāga*) refers to a white female dog. “Power” (*śakti*) refers to a *byar ba*. “The wound of an arrow” (*iṣu-vraṇa*) refers to a bee. “Struck” (*tāḍita*) means beaten. “One’s own seed” (*svabīja*) refers to one’s own property. “Victory” (*jaya*) refers to a victory in dice. “Born woman” (*janitri*) refers to a woman. “Seizing the unfortunate” (*durbhaga-grahaṇa*) means taking hold of. “Male tree” (*pādapa*) refers to the mango tree (*āmra*) and so forth. “Tree branch” (*vṛkṣa-śākhā*) refers to a leaf. “*Pilu*” refers to an elephant. “Leading upward” (*ūrdhva-nayana*) means holding with the hand. “Intoxicant for men” (*puruṣa-madana*) refers to a substance. “*Kranta*” refers to the suppression of Viṣṇu. “*Śrabaṇṭī*” refers to smoke. “*Ābaṃtajatikā*” refers to joining the palms together. “*Śikhā*” refers to the crest of a peacock. “Lord of the ḍākinīs” (*ḍākinī-pati*) refers to the lord of the garuḍas (*khagendra*). “Secret of the Lord of Gods” (*devapati-guhya*) refers to Indra-guhya. “*Ba bla*” refers to *maṃśila*. “*Ldong ros*” refers to blue *ljong ros*. “*Au kra*” refers to a calf. “Born after being burned” (*dagdha-jāta*) refers to a durva grass. “Auspicious” (*maṅgala*) refers to *rocanā*.

Baccha, fresh *indrayava* from outside, *kuṭabīja* (or in some places *phuṭabīja*), *śrīśalaka*, *dāruvarṇa*, red sandalwood (*aruṇacandana*), *raktacandana*, *ṛṣisuta*, *khaga*, *khañjanaka*, *girika*, *karṇikā*, *aparājita*, *srota* (or *srotāñjana*), *saṃkaṭa*, *kaṇṭaka*, *sevāla-kaṇṭaka*, honey (*madhu*), *mākṣika*, *madhuka*, *madhuyaṣṭī*; the first menstrual blood of a young woman; "three metals" (*triloha*) refers to gold, silver, and copper.
triloham; [the editor's emendation], trilokam (as in W)

*Āma* means the manifestation of the navel. *Indrayava* is the seed of *kūṭaja*; for some, it is the seed of *kuṭaja*. *Sarvaśrī* is that which possesses beauty. *Arjunā* is red sandalwood. *R̥ṣiputra* refers to those who travel through the sky and those born from space. *Śailarāja* is the invincible. *Spodā* is an ointment for the eyes. *Śaśakalakṣaṇakaṇṭaka* is the thorn of the *sephālikā*. *Madhu* is honey. *Madhuka* is the honey of the *yaṣṭi* plant. *Prathamapuṣpa* is the blood of the first menses. "The three metals" refers to gold, silver, and copper.

The *aśoka* tree characterized by its blueness is the "blue *aśoka*" (*nīlāśoka*). Its light-sprout is the "light-sprout of the blue *aśoka*" (*nīlāśokaprabhāṅkura*), meaning the sprout-house. Blood; the sun is copper, the moon is silver, fire is gold. *Gorocanā* is the bile of cows. The flower of the *iṅgudī* tree is the "flower of the *iṅgudī* tree" (*iṅgutītarukusuma*); this is a collection. The eye-hairs of one who has come from the *amṛtā* plant after being bound; joined with the two that have passed away, joined with those discarded after being eaten twice. A cemetery is a charnel ground (*śmaśāna*); there, it is "strengthened" (*marddhita*) by the semen extracted from a menstruating girl. It is both blue and sorrowful, thus "blue-sorrow" (*nīlāśoka*). To its north is the nest of the crow, the abode of crows. Those sprouts manifested there are the "sprouts of the crow-nest in the northern direction of the blue *aśoka*" (*nīlāśokottaradigvāyasanīḍāṅkurāḥ*).

"Blue" (*nīla*) is that which is characterized by and associated with blueness; "aśoka tree" is the *aśoka* tree. "Sprout arising from that" means a sprout arising from the blue *aśoka* tree. "The sun" is copper-colored, meaning intensely red. "The moon" is silver. "Fire" is gold. "Bull's urine" is the urine of a bull. "Flower of the *iṅgudī* tree" refers to the *kusuma* of the *iṅgudī* forest tree—that is, the flowers of all forest trees collectively. "Obstacle" refers to a dead man; [it consists of] his eyes and hair. "Possessed by one who has been eaten by a crow" means vomited up after being eaten by a crow, leaving no remainder. "The father’s garden" is the charnel ground (*śmaśāna*). "Taking the substance of a girl intoxicated by her monthly menses" means enjoying her there. "That which is both an *aśoka* and blue" is the blue *aśoka*. "The northern ravine of that" is the dwelling place of ravens. "Whatever sprout arises from that" is the sprout of the northern ravine of the blue *aśoka* tree.

Srotāñjana (antimony) placed within the belly of a pigeon, when heated by the fire of a funeral pyre, becomes *asidvāñjana* (black antimony). [It is processed] with the excrement of a black cat and the blood of a black cat; thus the visibility of the secret [vision] arises. The fresh butter is thickened, and the grass sprouts are dense forest-grass. [From the phrase] *kiloparisthāyā*: it is provided with a tube of dead essence (*mṛtasāraghatana*), namely *sāragha* (honey), *mākṣika* (bee-honey), and *tāla* (orpiment); these combined and joined together are "provided with honey and orpiment" (*sāraghātālānvitā*). On the day of Puṣya, the ointment is applied [as previously described].
[Haritālam] arises from those two.
The scribe has confused the folios in his exemplar!

One should place *sro ta* and *āmjana* inside a hollowed-out ant-hill, yet they must be burned by the fire of *jita*. Thereby, the eye medicine will be accomplished. That which was killed by a cat that is not white is rendered invisible by the blood of a black cat; this is for the purpose of generating a corpse. "A cluster of fresh *trina* sprouts" refers to a collection of fresh *trina* sprouts. "The ground trampled by those" means the ground trampled by a cluster of fresh *tāla* sprouts. "The ground situated upon that," "the wound of an arrow," and "possessing *tāla*" [are the components]. "The wound of an arrow" refers to bees; "*tāla*" refers to resin. Being "properly endowed" with these means being accompanied by *saraga* and *tāla*. "On the day of victory" means on the day of the sun of victory (*vijayārkadine*). The "eye medicine" is as described above.

By means of this mantra, the accomplishment of the medicinal compound (*oṣadhisaṃyoga*) occurs through the application of yoga. This sequence of the yoga-mantra has come down [traditionally]; therefore, it is said that one should accomplish it within the *bhaga*. First, having empowered the *mudrā*, one should subsequently insert the preparation of the collyrium (*añjana*) and meditate upon its union until the signs of accomplishment have arisen. He says that even without the accomplishment of the heart-mantra, this collyrium alone performs pacification (*śānti*) and other rites. Having anointed the eyes, one should look with a gaze of pacification and so forth; pacification and the rest will occur. Having anointed the eyes, one should look at a king; one receives honor from the king. Having anointed the eyes, one should look at an enemy with a wrathful gaze; the destruction of the enemy occurs. In the same way, one should gaze upon all obstacles. He says that all obstacles, such as planetary spirits (*graha*), are utterly severed when one recites the mantra after consecrating it with the mantra to be explained. Having thrown saffron (*kuṅkuma*) into the womb of a woman, and then having entered one’s own practice, one should recite the mantra using the "enclosure" (*saṃpuṭa*) yoga and thus accomplish it—this is the distinction.

If one performs [the rite] well through the application of mantras and medicinal herbs, it will be accomplished by that very application. These [methods] originate from the Yoga Tantras; therefore, it is said: "Then, one should perform the accomplishment within the *bhaga*. First, having consecrated the mudrā, one should subsequently insert the eye-salve (*añjana*) and meditate through its application for as long as the signs of accomplishment (*siddhi*) have not arisen. It is said: "Even this eye-salve alone, when devoid of mantra-accomplishment, performs activities such as pacification (*śānti*) and so forth. Having anointed the eyes with eye-salve, if one gazes with the gaze of pacification and so forth, pacification and the like will occur. Having anointed the eyes with eye-salve, if one gazes at a king, the king will obtain offerings. Having anointed the eyes with eye-salve, if one gazes at an enemy with a wrathful gaze, the enemy will be devoured. Likewise, if one gazes decisively at all obstructors, all obstructors such as spirits (*graha*) and so forth will be completely driven away. It is said: "One should recite and chant [the mantra] while consecrating it with the mantra of severance. Having placed *gur gum* (red sandalwood) into the *bhaga* of a woman, one should subsequently insert one's own practice (*svasādhana*) and, through union, chant the mantra and accomplish it until it is exhausted.

He spoke that mantra which was indicated: *Oṃ prasannatāre amṛtamukhi amṛtalocane sarvārthasādhani sarvasattvavaśaṅkari hūṃ phaṭ haṃ svāhā* (ending with *svāhāṃ*). *O three-faced, six-armed goddess Māmakī of fierce form, hrīṃ 2 hūṃ 2 aṃ 2 haḥ 2 svāhā!* It is said that after first performing one hundred thousand recitations as preliminary service (*pūrva-sevā*), one should subsequently accomplish the application of collyrium and saffron. He says that one should make a mark (*tilaka*) on the forehead with that saffron. Regarding the making of women auspicious: having written the syllable *bhrūṃ* with yellow orpiment (*gorocanā*) upon the vulva smeared with sandalwood paste, one should engage in union with the husband; until my arrival, that husband becomes submissive like a servant.

The recitation of its mantra was thus commanded: *Oṃ prasaṇnatāre āmr̥ta mukhi āmr̥talocane sarvārthasādhanī sarvasattvavaśaṅkari hūṃ phaṭ hāṃ svāhā | Oṃ timukhe śṭobhu dze devi māmakī rūpiṇī hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ āṃ āṃ hā hā svāhā*. It is said that after first reciting the preliminary service (*puraścaraṇa*) one million times, one should subsequently prepare eye-salve and also cultivate *gur-gum* (stereospermum). It is further stated that with that *gur-gum*, one should apply a drop (*tilaka*) upon the forehead. The command for making women fortunate was thus given: having written the syllable *brūm* with elephant ichor (*gajamada*) upon a base smeared with sandalwood, through union with the master [the practitioner], [the woman] will remain under his influence for as long as she does not become intoxicated [by passion]. Thereafter, that master shall become like a servant.

O King, *bhṛṅgarāja* is the king-bee; *sahasrapatrikā* is the female servant; *rajanī* is turmeric; *vāgujī* is *arakta*; *utpalasārī* is the bud of the blue lotus; *lohapurīṣā* is iron excrement; *gandhādi* is the resin of *guggulu*; *raktā* is *karmaraṅga*; *kanakadruma* is golden wood; *dṛḍhaprarohā* is the young shoot; *sindhucāru* is *nirguṇṭhī*; *śyāmā* is *priyaṅgu*; *keśara* is *nāgakeśara*; *vidyādharī* is *campaka*; *nāga* is *puṃnāga*; *cakramardha* is *eḍacī*; *niśācarī* is turmeric; *śikhi* is the crest of the peacock; *pravara* is *bālaka*; *bhūtāri* is *nirguṇṭhī*; *parahṛdvallabhī* is considered to be the flower-thief (*cauryapuṣpikā*); *karāra* is *karaja*; *mañjarī* is *dūmanaka*; *hematarutvaca* is bark; *ghana* is *mustaka*; *dārusamari* is *dāru*; *rajenadra* is *kuṣṭha*; *bhavanarajas* is house-flower; *cora* is *vṛddhadāraka*; and *keṃsu* is its ripe fruit.

*Nṛi-ba* is the king of *bung-ba*. *Tziti* is the thousand-petaled [lotus]. *Mtsan-mo* is *yung-ba*. *Ba-ku-tzi* is *ābā-gutza*. The heart of *autpala* is the unopened *autpala* flower. The stain of iron is the explanation of iron. "Fragrance and so forth" refers to *gu-gul* and *sajjara-sa*. "Blood flowing" is the color of karma. The golden tree is the golden grove-tree. *Dīdhapra-roha* is *pala*. *Sindhu-vara* is *nir-kunda*. *Śramā* is *priyāmku*. *Keśari* is *nāga-ge-sar*. The *vidyādhara* is *campaka*. *Nāga* is *bu-na-nāga*. *Cakrāvarta* is *ādiza*. "Practicing at night" is *yung-ba*. *Shikhi* is the crest of a peacock. *Pravara* is *bālāka*. *Bhūta-dvīpa* is *niraku-ta*. *Varahrida* is said to be the thief-flower of *ballabhida*. *Karākara* is *karana-dza*. *Manjarī* is that which subdues. The bark of the golden tree is *pag-sa*. *Ghana* is *mustaka*. The tree of night is the *skyer-ba* tree. The lord of disease is *kunda*. The dust of existence is the house-flower. The thief is the one who makes the old young. *Kem-su* is its fully ripened fruit.

For those engaged in the practice of constructing mandalas and so forth, the Māras such as Devaputramāra may sometimes cause obstructions; therefore, he teaches all the weapon-mudrās for the purpose of dispelling them.
Regarding the performance of practices such as the mandala and so forth, in order to subdue certain obstacles such as the *devaputra-māra* that may arise: "The great mudrās of all weapons:
those released from a mechanical device (*yantra*), those not yet released, likewise those released by the hand, those released and then supported, and fifthly, hand-to-hand combat."
The self-arisen science of archery (*dhanurveda*) consists of five techniques:
the discharge of the mechanical bow, the discharge without a mechanical device, likewise the discharge by hand,
the catching of what has been discharged, and fifthly, hand-to-hand combat.
Since the bow has become self-arisen through knowledge, one should firmly establish the mudrā.

In this context, "released by a machine" refers to arrows and the like; "unreleased" refers to swords and the like; "released from the hand" refers to discuses and the like; and "supported by what has been released" refers to nooses and the like. When all weapons have been abandoned, there is hand-to-hand combat involving the binding of enemies, wives, and so forth; likewise, the excellent missiles were taught by the venerable Vajrasattva. I shall now explain the arrangement of the Universal Noose (*viśvapāśa*): the yoga of *+ai* and *+ṣṭa*; there is no excellence or lightness in [ordinary] beings. Attraction, retention, and clearly liberation—[one should] seal the earth with the even-footed stance (*samapada*), seal the ground with the *vaiśākha* stance, and seal the mandala with the *ālīḍha* stance, which is the blessing of the three worlds.

Regarding those [weapons] such as the bow launched from a sling, and those not launched such as the sword; those held in the hand such as the wheel, and those together with the holder such as the noose—having completely set aside all such weapons, one should slay the enemy with the striking of the hands. Likewise, one should be fully equipped with bonds. I shall now thoroughly explain the various locations and forms of the supreme weapons of the glorious Vajrasattva. The yoga-sādhana is exceedingly beautiful: joining, swift piercing, summoning, and holding itself; emitting clearly, and stamping upon the earth with the mudrās. One stamps the *beśakhā* (the fresh corpse) with the mudrās, and stamps that very maṇḍala with the mudrās. One extends the right [leg] toward the three places.

He speaks of the *saṃsthānamudrā* (posture-seal): "When the heels are eight finger-breadths apart, joined and firm, they call that the 'even-footed' (*samapada*) stance. When both feet are placed with the outer toes touching, the knees stiff and slightly moving, that even-footed stance is called *vaiśākha*. Where the two knees are remembered to be level, shaped like the wings of a swan, and separated by a distance of two cubits, that stance is known as *maṇḍala*. When the right knee and thigh are stiff and shaped like a fruit, while the left is extended sideways and the shanks remain aligned, its width being five spans (*vitasti*), that is proclaimed as *ālīḍha*. That same position reversed is proclaimed as *pratyālīḍha*. Lack of laxity, stability, softness, firmness of limb, and the purity of the full dimensions—this is the well-proportioned *kāyamudrā* (body-seal). By means of this, which adorns all limbs, fevers, passions, poisons, diseases, *ḍākinīs*, and whatever *grahas* there may be, do not prevail in any way. This is the *pūrṇāyatanamudrā*."

The Instruction on the Mudrās of the Sky: The thumbs and the fingers are joined within the hollow of the palms. That which is joined firmly is said to be the stance of the even feet. Having placed the toes of the feet outward and straightened the two knees, with a measurement of twenty-six finger-widths, this stance is called *bhaiṣākharu*. With the mudrā of the swan’s wings, the two knees are joined evenly; the distance between them is exactly two cubits. This is taught as the stance for the maṇḍala. Furthermore, in the even mudrā of the plow, if one protects the right side of the thighs with the knees, the left is the gait of a beast. Having encircled [the body], they rest upon the thighs and chest; expanded to a height of five [cubits], that is renowned as the *pratyālīḍha* (right-extended) stance. The exact opposite of that is called the *ālīḍha* (left-extended) stance. Neither relaxed nor rigid, supple and with firm limbs—by means of which the sense bases (*āyatana*) are purified—this great mudrā of one’s own body [overcomes] diseases of the humors, poisons, the terrors of ḍākinīs, and malevolent spirits. Adorned with all these limbs, it overpowers everything. This is the mudrā of the full sense bases.
Having grasped the bow with great elegance through the method of drawing it toward one’s own heart,
and having drawn back the arrow with the right hand, one succeeds in its discharge. This indeed is the discharge.
Having made the left arm level with the right, one should slowly draw back the left breast; whoever performs this draws in the entire world. This is the Sarvākarṣaṇamudrā (the Seal for Drawing All).

Through the yoga of summoning the heart-essence, one should grasp the bow with great beauty; by turning it well to the right and piercing with the arrow, success will be achieved. Having placed the hands together in front and drawn them back toward the back, one should slowly summon whomever is to be summoned; thus all beings are to be summoned. This is the mudrā for summoning all.

Having raised [the hand] according to rule, with the eyes reaching as far as the ears, one should hold one’s own face [in the form of] a mere *tuṃkāra*. One should hold it for as long a time as it takes to utter the syllable *oṃ*. This is the *dharaṇa-mudrā* (the mudrā of retention). "Having placed [the hand] into the mandala of the sense bases (*āyatana*), In the proper sequence, one should hold the syllable *oṃ* For as long as one maintains it oneself; For that duration of time, one should recite *oṃ*. This is the mudrā of retention."

Having drawn [the breath] in according to the rule, one should hold it according to the ritual procedure; one should cause it to expand slightly therein, and when fully filled, success is attained. This is the *pūraṇa-mudrā*. Having covered [the mouth] with the fist, and having placed the gaze and the fist upon the face, by releasing [the breath], the supreme [attainment] is accomplished. This is the *dhanur-vijaya-mudrā*.

Smiling and gazing with the eyes, one should direct the gaze toward the target; having adopted this posture and directed the gaze, by drinking [the nectar] thoroughly, the supreme accomplishment will be attained. This is the mudrā of victory by means of the bow.

Square, sharp, and likewise turned away; one should wrap with the left hand, [placed] low and reaching the head. In the sequence of treading and the harsh treading, by means of this *graha-mudrā*, one enjoys the bliss of the great sovereignty over the three realms. This is the *Śrītrailokyavijit-svayaṃ-mudrā*. Cast forward, cast equally, and likewise cast like lightning; and also whirled like lightning—this is the *mudrā* that accomplishes attraction. With the hands level and downward, and likewise reaching the directions and the head, one should then meditate upon the three worlds through the *dhāraṇī-mudrās*. The *Sarvābharaṇa-mudrā*: everywhere, from all sides, everything, in every way, at all times, and by oneself. "The supreme syllable, the excellent *mudrā* of the science of archery (*dhanurveda*), is accomplished. This is the *Sarvāyudha-mudrā*.

A square, a sharp [triangle], and a circle; likewise, one should perform the supreme circumambulation. Wherever one should arrange [the gestures] from the right, one should likewise proceed below and above. By pressing and forcefully pressing in sequence, through the ten rites, one attains the supreme seal (*mudrā*). One enjoys the great sovereignty over the three realms and the bliss of the Victorious One. The faithful *Trailokyavijaya* (Victor of the Three Worlds), having applied the seal and entered into equipoise, likewise applies it like a flash of lightning. Through the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of drawing in the seal, one likewise performs the circumambulation like a flash of lightning. Just as one enters below, one likewise proceeds toward the upper direction. This is the seal for holding the Tathāgatas; one should visualize it in the three places. This is the seal of all ornaments. In every way, from everywhere, at all times, and in every respect, one holds the bow-vidyā seal of oneself. The supreme syllable will be accomplished. This is the seal of all weapons.

"Buddhavajra" refers to Vairocana. Together with Locanā, Rūpā, and Mudrā, one who possesses the yoga of Vairocana should visualize Locanā emerging from the syllables of her mantra, holding a full moon and a water-pot in her hands, sprinkling the interior [of the mandala], and thus become the mother of peace. She bestows life even upon the dead and grants accomplishment to those who have attained it.

The one called Buddha Vajra is Vairocana; having become the form of the eye, and by means of the yoga of Vairocana, one should draw forth the eye from the mantra-syllable. Visualizing a full moon and the *kalaśa* in the hand of the Mother—the Māmakī—and performing the consecration, one generates pacification. This bestows life upon those who have died and grants the desired object to those who seek accomplishment.

"Vajra," and so forth: it is called "the exhortation of the Vajra-samaya" because it exhorts the Vajra-samaya. It refers to that samādhi in which the supreme samaya of the Mind-Vajra—which has been purified by the three bodies—is characterized by Māmakī. Having emitted the seed-syllables of the mantra of the Vajra family, one should then visualize the body of the sādhya as being full; [this visualization] shall be the destroyer of evil.

Regarding the phrase "Vajra" and so forth: that which exhorts the vajra-samaya is the "exhortation to the vajra-samaya. The supreme samaya of the blazing three bodies of the Mind-Vajra is the characteristic of Māmakī; wherever one is in meditative absorption, it is described as such. Having emitted the white syllables of the mantra of the Vajra family, if one visualizes them filling the body of the object of accomplishment at that time, it will destroy all negativity.

One should effect peace for the afflicted person like Locanā. For nourishment (*puṣṭi*), one should visualize [Amitābha] emitting a rain of jewels from a jewel-filled flask. Amitābha is Great Passion (*mahārāga*). His dance—the blossoming—of the lotus by which he has conquered passion (*raṃ*) belongs to him who is bowed down. That which produces all activities arising therefrom is of the nature of his own family; because all non-activities are scattered by it, the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) based on that is likewise said to be of the nature of Vajrabala. *Ai* is the vajra-lotus of Amitābha. Having emitted golden-colored mantra-syllables, one should consecrate the object of practice (*sādhya*). This generates great nourishment. One should meditate on those very syllables through their radiation and reabsorption; this increases the treasury of Dharma. Having placed the garland of the object’s mantra-syllables within the pericarp of one's own heart and topped it with a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*), and having performed union (*samāpatti*) according to the rule, one performs the great activity of protection.

For pacification, one should visualize the Guru as having eyes like those of a wrathful mother; for enrichment, one should contemplate a rain of jewels falling from a precious vase. For great passion, one should visualize the lotus upon which Amitābha sits being opened by his dance; the agent who acts in this way possesses the nature of the lord of all families, and that which he performs is everything. By focusing on what has been performed through this visualization, one likewise speaks of focusing on the vajra within meditative absorption (*samādhi*). The "vajra" is Vairocana; the "lotus" is Amitābha. Having emitted mantra-syllables with a color like gold, if they confer empowerment upon the practitioner, they generate a great king. If one meditates on their emanation and reabsorption, the treasury of the Dharma will increase. If one visualizes the object of accomplishment dwelling within the center of the lotus at one's own heart, empowered by a garland of mantra-syllables, and enters into meditative equipoise while placing various vajras upon the crown of the head, it will provide great protection.

All masteries, such as the mastery of non-conceptuality and so forth, are awakened by him; he is Amoghavajrī. He is that very equality of the three vajras. Having entered that samādhi which possesses the indestructible vajra that causes delight in that [equality], and having emitted the red mantra-syllables and filled the object to be accomplished with them, he should recite it; thus he makes [the deity] his servant.

Because he has mastery over all things, he is free from conceptual construction; yet, through that very mastery and so forth, he engages in conceptualization and brings [the goal] to birth—he is the one who possesses the meaningful vajra. He is the one who brings joy through the equality of the vajra speech. "Vajra" means indivisible; by entering into meditative absorption (*samādhi*) therein, the red syllables of the mantra overflow, and when one performs the recitation to purify what is to be accomplished, they bring about the entry of the command.

The introduction to knowledge (*jñānāvatāraṇatā*)... because it is the object of focus for that [knowledge], it is so described. The "guide of knowledge" (*jñānanetrī*) refers to the diversity of supramundane knowledge, such as the wrathful deities Vajrayamāntaka and others, who are indeed those [deities] placed within cages for the sake of subduing the wicked. "Beautiful," "great," "limb," "one," "fragment," and "two-streamed"—thus it is "two-fragmented" (*dvikhaṇḍa*), because these two alone are the subject at hand.

She is called "Tārā" (the Saviouress) because she liberates all through primordial wisdom (*jñāna*); she is the one who causes primordial wisdom to enter. At that time, it is spoken of in that way for the sake of being its object of focus. "Various primordial wisdoms" refers to the various supramundane primordial wisdoms; the wrathful deities such as Vajrayamāntaka and others are themselves those [wisdoms] for the purpose of subduing the malevolent ones, and they are the very *guhya* (the secret/enclosure). "Beautiful" means that her limbs and minor members are not deficient. "Without joints" means having a single joint; "with two joints" means having two joints, because these are the specific contexts for these [deities].

"By means of the dust from the feet" means this: the yogin of Yamāntaka, possessing the yoga of the four goddesses and empowered by the five Tathāgatas, takes the dust from the feet of the person to be subdued (*sādhya*), places it inside a skull-cup, and having brought that very person in, bound them, and stepped upon them with his left foot, he should recite the mantra accompanied by the exhortation until she is summoned.

The ritual of the dust from the footprint, known as "The Ritual of the Dust from the Footprint," is explained as follows: A practitioner of Yamāntaka, endowed with the yoga of the four goddesses and empowered by the five Tathāgatas, should fashion an image using the dust from a footprint to be accomplished. This should be placed inside a skull-cup; having performed the rites of insertion and binding, one should press it down with the left foot and recite the mantra while exhorted, until it is completely crushed.

"By means of the meditations on the radiance of the three bodies" means: [it refers to] the firm *ahaṃkāra* (I-am-ness) of one's own deity... [omitted] ...O foremost among those free from delusion, O Amoghavajrī! His noble gnosis is the bodhicitta arisen from the vajra. Therefore, the "Vajrāmṛtakrodha" is that samādhi in which this [gnosis] exists; thus it is so called.

Regarding the phrase "by meditating on the indivisibility of the three *skus*," this means that one meditates with firm divine pride (*devatā-māna*) as one's own deity. Amoghasiddhi is the supreme among those of great delusion; his gnosis is the bodhicitta born from the vajra-point. Therefore, the "nectar-anger" (*amṛta-krodha*) is designated as such in accordance with that very meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

"Offered at the feet of Gaṇapati!"—thus, one who possesses the yoga of Amṛtakuṇḍalin should fashion an image of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) out of dust and donkey urine. Having written the name of the *sādhya* interspersed with the *krodha*-mantra upon leaves of the *vātamaṇḍalī* tree using charcoal from a cremation ground mixed with flour, one should bind that image at five points with a *vajra-vināyaka*. Having invoked and fully worshipped [the deity], one should offer it at his feet; this is the meaning. And at the end of the mantra, one should utter "hūṃ."

When there is an obstruction by wind, then, having focused on emptiness according to the previously mentioned sequence and visualizing oneself in the form of Śrī Vairocana, one says: "Vāyavya... [A168 recto]. Within a square mandala of black fragrance, there are seven drops, each separated from the others by the letter *ya*. In the center is the seventh drop; these seven drops are the seven winds, mounted on deer and black in color. There, generated from the seven seed-syllables, they are drawn in by that very [deity], bound with a noose by the immovable Ṭakkirāja, and should be visualized. Then, with a shallow bowl in the form of Mount Sumeru possessing eight peaks and facing downward, one utters the mantra of oneself—*vajramahābandha*—and should suppress the sevenfold mantra with a hidden breath, saying *hūṃ suṃ hūṃ*.

Regarding the phrase "placing [the victim] at the feet of the Gaṇapati": one who possesses the yoga of the *amṛtakuṇḍalī* (nectar-arrangement) should fashion an image of the footprints of the person to be accomplished using the dung of a donkey. Having formed this into an "inauspicious mudrā," one should carve *śālu* roots from the petals of a wind-maṇḍala. One should write the name of the person to be accomplished in the midst of a wrathful deity using charcoal from a charnel ground, and having placed five images behind it, one should summon Vajra-Viparita (the "wrongly-guiding vajra"), worship him, and place [the victim] at his feet. The phrase "one should do that" means that until that point, one should utter the syllable *hūṃ* at the end of the mantra. When the wind becomes an obstacle, at that time, one should visualize emptiness according to the sequence previously described and generate oneself in the form of Śrī Vairocana. It is taught: in the direction of the wind, within a square maṇḍala, there are seven bindus inside each of the seven *ya* letters; these seven bindus are the seven Wind-Gods (*vāyu-deva*), dark-colored and riding upon mountain goats. From their respective seed-syllables, they are emanated—that is, they are projected from one's own heart by Ārya Acala or Kāmarāja. One should imagine them having arrived and bound [the victim]. Then, regarding the phrase "with a skull-cup": from the syllables *hūṃ sum hūṃ*, one generates the form of Mount Meru with eight peaks. By piercing the mouth downward and placing it [over the victim], this is the "great vajra-binding. Reciting one's own mantra means that the seven bindus of that [victim] are concealed by the mantra and made to abide through the breath.

Above that, by means of the syllable *laṃ*, one should visualize a yellow, square Ā-maṇḍala of Indra, which is stepped upon by a terrifying wrathful vajra with five large prongs radiating continuous rays of light. Having placed the left foot upon it, one should recite the mantra of Noble Acala one hundred and eight times. Thus, above the vajra, one should visualize the Blessed One Vairocana and Noble Acala, who, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, presses down upon the mountain; the Blessed One’s hand holds a sword and a noose, and his wisdom-light... [by this] even the entire wind of the time of universal dissolution is bound.
% NB parallel to Ānandagarbha’s *Sarvavajrodayā*!

Above that, one should visualize a four-sided mandala of the Great Wind, yellow in color. From a great five-pronged [vajra] there, infinite rays of light emanate terrifying wrathful deities, and one should meditate on these wrathful ones pressing down with vajras. Placing the left foot upon that, one should recite the mantra of the Noble Acala one hundred and eight times. Upon the vajra, one should visualize the Bhagavān Vairocana and the Noble Acala pressing down everything with their right legs extended; one should imagine that the Bhagavān holds a sword in his hand and, with his breath, fans the wind. By doing so, all the winds of the time of terror will be bound.

For the sake of virility, having drawn an eight-petalled lotus with the words "O you of great strength" (*mahābala*) and so forth, one should sequentially place upon its eight petals the eight *nāgas*: Ananta, Kulika, Vāsuki, Śaṅkhapāla, Takṣaka, Mahāpadma, Karkoṭaka, and [the eighth]. Two are yellow and two are white; they possess the syllables *sa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*, and each is presided over by its own seed-syllable. Having invoked and worshipped these eight *nāgas* situated within the pericarp, one should then contemplate oneself as the form of the Wrathful One (*krodha*)—a mass of blazing flames—reciting *m-hūṃ naṃ hūṃ*. One should visualize [the deity] pressing down upon the surface of the earth. One should also contemplate the *nāgas* as intent on releasing water for the purpose of sustaining the rain. Contemplating oneself in the form of the Wrathful One, possessing a beautiful luster like that of a great red sun, one should split open one's own mouth, which is immeasurable in the sky and has a tongue blazing with the syllable *hūṃ*. Having licked the clouds filled with [rain], one should expel them through exhalation like cotton wool. Alternatively, emitting a blazing host of one's own mudrās, one should rend and sever them, intent on the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) of the syllable *hūṃ*.
Somewhere here, a correction should be applied from the lower margin: "adbhir iti a + + +".

Regarding the passage beginning with “For the purpose of causing rain, one should perform the rite called ‘The Very Powerful’” (*Char 'bab pa'i don du stobs po che zhes bya ba la sogs pa ni*): having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, on its eight petals one should invoke the eight *nāgas*—Ananta, Kulika, Vasuki, Śaṅkhapāla, Takṣaka, Mahāpadma, Balaha, and Padma—by means of their respective seed-syllables, *śa śa sa hā svām svā sāṃ svāḥ*, which are yellow and white according to the sequence of oneself. Having summoned them into the interior of the eight essences (*snying po*) within the drum, one should worship them. Then, if one meditates that the host of blazing wrathful deities residing in this [mandala] are uttering the supreme recitation of *hūṃ hūṃ*, thereby subduing the *nāgas* beneath their feet, rain will fall most excellently. Regarding the instruction for stopping the rain: one should visualize oneself as the form of a wrathful deity, intensely red like the color of the sun. With a blazing *hūṃ* at one's own mouth, one should split and completely fill the expanse of space. From this, the clouds are drawn in by the suction of the breath from the hollow of the heart; then, as the breath is expelled, they are scattered like cotton wool. Alternatively, one should split and cut [the clouds] by raising the assembly of one's own blazing mudrās, and then utterly incinerate them with *hūṃ*.

For the purpose of pacifying all obstacles, he says: "The one endowed with the eternal yoga," and so forth. One should visualize [the deity] as possessing six arms, situated within a circle of fire arising from the syllable *Raṃ* that has emerged from his own forehead and originated from the noble Acala. On the left, he holds a noose marked by the syllable *Kṣīṃ* and entwined with the syllable *Hūṃ*; on the right, a bow marked by the syllable *Dha*. With the syllable *Kha*, he holds a sword; with the syllable *Hoḥ*, [a wheel]; and with the syllable *Hūṃ*, he holds a vajra. Having visualized him thus, together with other wrathful deities (*krodhas*), one should pierce all human obstacles with the sound of the *Hūṃ* of Sarvavighnāntaka, using weapons such as the sun-stone, the sword, and so forth, and by the discharge of arrows.

Regarding the instruction on the meaning of destruction, starting with the phrase "the fire mandala" and so forth: one who possesses the yoga of permanence should emanate from their own forehead the noble Lord Acala, arisen from the syllable *raṃ*. Residing within the fire, he has six arms; his left hand, marked by the syllable *kṣīṃ*, forms the threatening mudrā, and its middle finger is inserted into the interior of the syllable *hūṃ*. With that [finger], he draws the bow. His right hands hold a sword from *khāṃ*, an arrow from *hoḥ*, and a vajra from *hūṃ*. Visualizing him thus, together with the wrathful deities of his light rays, one should subdue all obstructing spirits (*bgegs*) by sounding the sound of *hūṃ* and striking them with the blazing sword and other weapons, and by piercing them with the discharged arrows. In this way, the obstructing spirits are to be overcome.

With the clay from the feet of a great man smeared with human blood, one should fashion an image of the target. Having performed the consecration twenty times with the *mārīci* mantra over two stakes made of human bone, one should pierce the eyes [of the image]. One should then visualize [the deity] entering the mouth of Gaṇapati and striking the back of the thunderbolt-mace with the mantra: *Oṃ sumbha vajramuṣalena...* For the purpose of removing the fire, one should employ the "color of collyrium" (*mañjanavarṇa*) and so forth. In the space of the sky, having formed a Garuḍa by interweaving the syllables *hūṃ gaṃ hūṃ*, surrounded by a thousand black serpents and acting upon the command of Tārkṣya, one should first issue the command with *Oṃ vajranārāyaṇa* and so forth, and through that, incite the enemy. He too, for the sake of raining down strength, should be made to give the command to the rain-clouds. Having heard the command, the clouds, while warding off the downpour of water, [are countered]; and Garuḍa, holding his wings, should create a boundary for the river with a blow of his beak.

Having fashioned an effigy to be accomplished using human blood and the dust from the footprint of a man, one should empower twenty-one kīla-stakes made of human bone with the mantra of Marīcī. Having driven these kīlas into the eyes [of the effigy], one should place it upon the seat of Gaṇapati. One should visualize that it is first struck on the mouth with a vajra-staff and a mallet, and then struck on the back with the staff. For the purpose of subduing the intermediate space, regarding the phrase "the medicinal color" (*sman gyi kha dog*) and so forth, one should place the syllable *hūṃ* within the expanse of space. From the seed-syllable *phuḥ*, one should command the Garuḍa surrounded by ten million black nāgas. Having visualized this exactly as it is, one should first incite him with the mantra *oṃ vajranārāyaṇa* and so forth; by that, even Indra should be incited. Furthermore, he should be commanded for the sake of rain toward the rain-clouds. If the command is heard, rain will fall. If one mentally intends to drive back the clouds, the wings of the Garuḍa will drive them away, and by striking with his beak, he will establish the boundary of the river.

He speaks of the "Vajra-Obstruction" (*vajranivāraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "the fire sacrifice," etc., "that which brings about auspiciousness" refers to the characteristics of pacification (*śānti*), enrichment (*puṣṭi*), and subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). One should perform [the rite] in a fire produced by churning. Furthermore, consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and so forth must also be performed. Regarding the "pit" (*kuṇḍa*), one should construct it as circular, square, semi-circular, or triangular; the meaning is that one should fashion [the hearths] situated upon white, yellow, red, and black lotuses, colored accordingly, with an *uṣṇīṣa*, a lotus, a jewel, a flame, and a vajra positioned below them.

The meaning of the *Vajravyāvartana* was thus taught. Regarding the phrase "the fire offering" (*homa*) and so forth: for the sake of performing virtuous deeds, one should employ the fire arising from ritual friction (*manthāna*) for the characteristics of pacification (*śānti*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), and magnetizing (*vaśya*). For the rite of wrathful activity (*abhicāra*), one should employ the fire of a charnel ground. As for the hearth (*kuṇḍa*), it is circular, square, semi-circular, or triangular. Accordingly, one should place white, yellow, red, and black lotuses around the perimeter of the hearth. Subsequently, according to their respective colors, one should fashion the ritual cakes (*bali*), water-born flowers, precious gems, and blazing vajras; such is the meaning.

"Regarding 'sarvaka + + + + m': it means consecrated by the syllable *hūṃ* with the left *vajra*. Having made the left hand into a three-pronged *vajra*, adorned with the rays of activity (*karmaraśmi*), one should transform it into the form of a flame, resplendent with the rays accumulated through activities such as pacification (*śānti*) and so forth. One should describe it as having the nature of gnosis (*jñāna*), in the form of a blazing garland of flames. One should utter the supreme mantra consisting of three parts, ending with *oṃ* and *svāhā*. For pacification, prosperity, and subjugation, however, one should [recite] together with the syllable *hūṃ* from the speech of the Wrathful One."

Regarding the phrase "by reciting the *las kun byed pa* (all-acting mantra)": it is that which is empowered (*abhimantrya*) with the syllable *hūṃ*. "Performing the vajra with the left hand" means making the left hand into a three-pronged vajra. "Adorned with the light of the activity" means appropriately embellished with the light of whichever activity is appropriate, such as pacifying (*śāntika*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "completely dissolved in the form of blazing": "blazing" refers to the deity, or the blazing form of the [deity]; in that way, one should meditate on the ritual of the nature of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). Having first established the *oṃ* at the beginning and *svāhā* at the end, for pacifying, increasing (*pauṣṭika*), magnetizing (*vaśya*), and wrathful activities (*abhicāruka*), one should recite the mantra with the assembly of wrathful deities together with *hūṃ phaṭ*.

One should offer [the oblation] at the beginning and the end, because of the statement "filling the mouth. One should offer it into the lotus-face of the deity; one should not suspect that there will be a blemish (*kalmāṣā*) in the offering of feces and urine, because all this is merely conceptual construction (*vikalpanāmātra*), being pure by nature (*svabhāvaśuddhatva*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). Even the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) generates uncontaminated knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) for one who, preceded by the ego-identification with the deity, brings about the single flavor (*ekarasa*) of wisdom and means. Showing that [this] is equal to the body, he says: "woman, man," etc., which demonstrates the procedure for the arising of karma for men who possess knowledge of the power of auspicious and inauspicious karma.

Regarding the phrase "filling the mouth," it means that the burnt offering (*homa*) should be made into the lotus of the deity’s face at the beginning and the end. One should not entertain apprehensions such as sin regarding the burnt offerings of excrement and so forth; for, in the ultimate sense, because their nature is utterly pure, everything is merely conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Likewise, by entering into the union of the two organs, one should first cultivate the divine pride (*devatāhaṃkāra*), realize the single taste of method and wisdom, and thereby generate uncontaminated gnosis (*anāsravajñāna*). As for the instruction on the perfect manifestation of the body and so forth, the passage beginning with "the bodies of women and men are produced by manifold actions" refers to a person who understands the characteristics of virtuous and non-virtuous karma. This is what is meant by "perfect manifestation."

Flesh, marrow, and so forth have Vairocana, Akṣobhya, and the others as their intrinsic nature; therefore, they are to be cultivated. Furthermore, those excretions such as feces and urine, which are free from the mental formations of passion, hatred, and so on—the five outflows—have the elements such as earth and so forth as their perfected intrinsic nature. Thus, by means of meditative cultivation, they are [realized] by those whose intellects are devoid of conceptual construction.

The head, feet, and so forth are the nature of Vairocana, Akṣobhya, and the other [Buddhas]; for this reason, they are the support. That which is described as the increase of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) called desire, hatred, and so forth, as well as the fivefold emission of excrement, urine, and so on, is the perfection of the nature of the four elements, earth and the rest. "From meditation" means by means of an intellect free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

Henceforth I shall explain the supreme universe in all its aspects, [extending] as far as the square [mandala] with four gates, provided with gatekeepers, and one should fashion the Gaṇamaṇḍala. Thus the outer maṇḍala has been described; now he shows the inner maṇḍala. "From the Viśvamudrā in every direction" refers to the goddesses such as Śrī Buddhalocanā and others. "From the Viśvacakrin in every direction" refers to Śrī Vajrasattva by means of the previously mentioned placement of the steps (*padanyāsa*). Following that, in the four directions and the four intermediate points, one should perform the ritual of *adhivāsana* for the deities of the maṇḍala by means of eight-finger-long stakes of *khadira* wood empowered by mudrās and mantras, using a vajra-hammer while reciting their respective mantras and striking them down. In the intermediate corners starting from the northeast, there are the stake-bindings known as Ananta, Vijaya, and so forth, in due order. One should thus consecrate the deities of the maṇḍala.
The supreme universe,
possessing four gates and provided with gatekeepers—
thus [is the description of] the exterior.
The maṇḍala has been described; [it is] the inner maṇḍala. From all sides, by means of the universal mudrās, [there are] the goddesses beginning with Śrī Buddhalocanā.

[in] the fourfold [set],
that mantra.

Now, the supreme [mandala] shall be explained: "The most diverse of all" refers to whatever [mandala] consists of four corners, four gates, and is perfectly endowed with gate-keepers. Regarding the phrase "the maṇḍala of the assembly should be examined," this speaks of the outer maṇḍala. Now, the inner maṇḍala will be shown. Regarding the phrase "the mudrā of the various [deities] of all," this refers to being endowed with the goddesses such as Śrī-Buddhalocanā and the others. Regarding the phrase "possessing the wheel of the various of all," one should arrange [the deities] in the place where Śrī-Vajrasattva is said to reside; subsequently, having empowered the four boundaries with the mantras and mudrās of Caṇḍā and the others, one should strike the center with an eight-finger-long khadira wood stake and a vajra hammer while reciting their mantras. Then, having driven in the stakes of Ananta, Vijayā, and so forth at the boundaries of Caṇḍā and the others in sequence, one should establish the maṇḍala deities in their positions.

Having consecrated the mandala ground with perfumes and other offerings, one should prepare a perfume-mandala (or *gaṇa*-mandala) at the locations of all the deities, preceded by the utterance of *svā*, the syllable *hūṃ*, and their respective names. Then, having emanated one’s own circle of deities and established them in their proper places, one should perform the [ritual] as prescribed, accompanied by one’s own mudrās and mantras, preceded by the act of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Having displayed [the offerings], conferred initiation, performed worship, and offered praise, one should prostrate and, for the sake of removing mental affliction, perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) and offer the directional bali.

With parched grain and other offerings, one should recite one’s own *hūṃ* and the first syllable of each deity’s name at the locations of all the deities of the maṇḍala, scattering them while visualizing them clearly. Having consecrated the root-vase and so forth in the proper manner, one should consecrate the disciples. First, having performed the *adhiṣṭhāna* (consecration) on the primary vase and so forth, one should perform the consecration for the disciples. After sprinkling water over the heart with water consecrated by the recitation of *Hūṃ*, one should place the hand together with a vajra upon it; one should visualize a five-pronged vajra at the heart and a *viśvavajra* (double-vajra) at the crown of the head for as long as necessary. Having performed the taking of refuge and so forth three times, and having bound the arms with a cord consecrated by *Hūṃ*, one should provide the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) and so forth, as well as the perfumes and other offerings. Having taught the Dharma to them, they should be led to the site of the maṇḍala; they should be requested to depart by means of its rays of light. The phrase "complete transformation as before" refers to performing the offerings and so forth. Just as the circle of deities was previously revealed, in that same manner, the circle of deities should be visualized within [the disciple]. This is the extent of the procedure.

Others, however, maintain that one who possesses the eternal yoga should emanate the hearts of Akṣobhya and the others, transform them into the five-colored threads beginning with blue, and upon the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*, perform the recitation one hundred and eight times; this same procedure applies to the colored powders (*rajas*) as appropriate. Introducing this very point, he says: "The master, having properly laid out the initial maṇḍala consecrated by the five Buddhas, should first perform the casting of the colored powders, and afterwards admit the disciples into the outer maṇḍala. In the [outer] circle, there are five types of colored powder: red, white, green, yellow, and black. In the second [circle], there are three: blue, red, and white. With the white powder, one should place at the nave of the wheel Mahāvairocana, seated upon a variegated and radiant lotus.

Furthermore, first, one endowed with the yoga of visualization should emanate Akṣobhya and the other [Buddhas] from their hearts, and having assumed the nature of those five cords of colors such as blue and so forth, one should slowly transform the syllable *Hūṃ* and recite it one hundred and eight times. Thus, it is taught that even for a sand mandala, one should employ this very yoga. After the five Buddhas have bestowed their blessings, the lines of the maṇḍala are drawn according to the directions. First, the preceptor (ācārya) should draw the sand mandala, and subsequently, the disciples [draw] the five types of colored powders—blue, red, white, green, and yellow—on the exterior of the maṇḍala. For the second [circle], there are three: blue, red, and white. As for the wheel, the center of the wheel is marked with white powder; regarding the "variegated blazing" [center], the Great Vairocana is to be seated upon a variegated lotus.

In the eastern and other cells, [one should place] Śāśvata and the others; in the eastern and other corners of the wheel, Locanā and the others; in the second enclosure (*puṭa*), in the eastern and other directions, Raudrī and the other Vajra-devis; and in the third enclosure, in the eastern and other quarters, one should draw Maitreya and the other Bodhisattvas. At every gate, [one should place] the Vajrāṅkuśa and others, and in the corners, [Locanā and] the others. Having thus drawn the maṇḍala, one should prepare eight hundred consecrated vases. One should make the root vase [consecrated] by the Lord of the Maṇḍala together with the four goddesses beginning with Locanā; it should be square, [and likewise] by all the deities according to their respective families. Furthermore, the sprinkling vase located at the door should be consecrated by the *sāmānyamantra*. Then, the practitioner, adorned with a body [purified] by bathing, clothing, and so forth, possessing the yoga of the Lord, and through the skillful yoga, having internalized the entire circle of deities within himself and maintaining the pride of being that [deity]:

In the *re'u mig* (diagrammatic squares) of the east and so forth are the permanent ones (*nityā*) and so on, according to their directions. In the intermediate points of the east and so forth of the wheel are Locanā and the others. In the directions of the east and so forth of the second enclosure are the fierce vajra goddesses, such as Caṇḍākṣī. On the cloths of the east and so forth of the third enclosure, the bodhisattvas Maitreya and the others are to be drawn. At the eastern gate are Vajrāṅkuśī and the others; in the intermediate points are Murajā and the others. In this manner, the maṇḍala is to be drawn. First, having properly prepared the vases, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. For the principal vase, it is the Lord of the Maṇḍala. For the fourth, it is by means of the four goddesses, Locanā and the others. There are four because of the classification of the families of all the deities. Then, for the vase situated at the gate, one should perform the purification offering (*vighnatarpaṇa*) by reciting the mantra of the All-Action (*sarvakarmaka*). Having adorned them with garments and so forth, possessing the yoga of the Lord, one should, through excellent yoga, visualize the entire wheel of all the deities within one's own self and maintain the pride (*ahaṃkāra*) of that.

Having opened the door that was obstructed by the arrangement of the *argha* offerings, and having placed the jars in their proper places, one should emanate the deities of the maṇḍala as before. Having established them in their own places, one should empower the wheel-deities and one's own deity with mudrās, display the binding mudrās, and consecrate them with one's own empowerment. Then, having visualized [the deities] as abiding in meditative absorption, one should worship them with all the offerings such as *lāsya* and so forth, and with delightful special offerings such as musical instruments and flutes. Having empowered them three times with the *vidyās* of empowerment while forming the hollow-palms gesture (*saṃpuṭāñjali*), one should sing praises with *vajragīti*. After bowing down for the sake of nourishment, since the fire sacrifice (*homa*) has been performed, one should ask for forgiveness.

Having completely recited the offerings for the *argha* (water for the feet), one should open the door. Having placed the vases and other items in their respective positions, one should emanate the deities of the maṇḍala as before and cause them to enter the wheel at their own places. Thinking that one abides in the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of self-empowerment through the thorough display of one’s own mudrās in order to empower [the deities] with the mudrās of one’s own deity, one should worship with the offerings of the graceful goddesses (*lāsyā*) and so forth. Then, having prostrated by means of the Vajra Song—well-composed and recited three times—with the palms joined by the *vidyā*-consorts who have empowered their own various pleasing offerings such as drums, cymbals, and the like, one should perform the fire offering (*homa*) spoken for the purpose of satisfaction, and thereafter request forbearance.

Then, for the sake of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*), having made the request and personally performed the preliminary rites and so forth, [the master] should prepare the disciples, adorned with bathing and other ornaments. Having performed everything according to the rule with the *oṃ* syllable and the heart-mantras, and having empowered them with the seals (*mudrā*) of the empowerment of the body, he should cause them to utter the *hūṃ* syllable in the form of a wheel with both hands joined in a hollowed gesture (*saṃpuṭāñjali*) with the index fingers encircled. Having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) at the five locations, their faces covered with cloth, they should enter with the *hūṃ* syllable alone by means of a flower accompanied by the seal of Vajradevī and the others. Then he should perform the entire general procedure. Having empowered the consecration vessel (*abhiṣeka-kalaśa*) as Vajrasattva and adorned it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, he should consecrate [the disciple] with the vases according to the rule.

Having made supplications for the sake of all *siddhis*, one should first generate [the deity] with the syllable *Oṃ* and so forth, and the disciple should be adorned with various ornaments. With *Oṃ* and so forth, one should perform the consecration of the body and so on at the heart, using the mudrās of blessing. Joining the palms in the form of a wheel with the index fingers extended, one should utter *Hūṃ* and apply it to all five places. Having covered the face with a cloth, one should enter with the *Hūṃ* itself and perform the general ritual using the mudrās of Vajradevī and so forth, holding flowers. Consecrated by the yoga of glorious Vajrasattva, one should be adorned with perfumes, flowers, and so on, and then consecrated with all the vases exactly as prescribed.

Having caused the Tathāgatas to emerge, one should see [the practitioner] being consecrated by them, who hold vases filled with divine nectar in their hands. Furthermore, having been adorned with garments and so forth, and consecrated by Akṣobhya and others transformed into various forms, [the master], standing near the cloth mandala, should consecrate him with the sovereignty of Vajra and the consecrations of the Vajra-name. Then, having removed the veil of ignorance with a golden or similar probe and taking up a mirror, he should explain the characteristics [of the Buddha-nature] with verses beginning: "The sentient being is by nature... and so forth.

One should visualize that the Tathāgatas offer libations and that the Vajrapāṇi Amṛtakuṇḍalin bestows empowerment upon them with water from vases. Furthermore, having adorned [the disciple] with garments and so forth, they are empowered by means of the vajra and other implements. Then, through the complete transformation of the forms of Akṣobhya and many others, there is the near-attainment of the skull-cup, the garland, the vajra, the master, and the vajra-name empowerment. With a golden or other ladle, the darkness of ignorance is dispelled. Taking up a mirror, one should proclaim the characteristics with verses such as, "The very nature of Vajrasattva," and so forth.

With the first vowel, one should give the book and the vajra-bell; with the [final] vowel, for the sake of granting permission, having empowered the feet, one should place the sword in the right hand and say: "From this day forth, turn the wheel for the world! One should address [the disciple] with the words beginning with "O Protector" (tāyin). Having sat down for the ritual commitment (samaya) beginning with "From this day forth," and having received the teacher’s fee (gurudakṣiṇā), one should perform the pacifying fire-offering (śāntika-homa). Having performed the worship, praise, and so forth, one should utter the syllable *HŪṂ*. Saying "Sattvavajrī, release!", one should dismiss the circle of deities.

First, with the first vowel (*ā*), one should hold up the volume; with the first consonant (*ka*), the vajra bell; and for the purpose of granting the authorization (*ājñā*), one should perform the consecration of the feet while bestowing the sword with the right hand. Then, holding it, one should visualize correctly, reciting "O Protector, turn the wheel of Dharma in the world," and so forth. With the words "From this day forward," and so on, the samaya is briefly taught. Having accepted the offerings from the Guru, one should perform the peaceful fire offering (*śānti-homa*). After performing the offerings, praises, and so forth, one should utter *Hūṃ*. With *Svā Vajra Muḥ*, one should request the assembly of deities to depart. *Oṃ*... [? *Gaccha*.

Having performed the ritual pinning (*kīlana*) and likewise the secret maṇḍala, one should dismiss [the deities] by means of the previously mentioned method while uttering *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*. Then, one should cause that which is thus distinguished to enter into its own place. One should effect the differentiation of the colored powders (*rajobheda*) with the syllable *hūṃ*. Having withdrawn [the maṇḍala], one should cast it into water. Regarding the arising of Śrī Heruka for the purpose of striking with the wrathful weapons of the wrathful ones, he says: "Thus that Blessed One," and so forth. This is called the "Initial Yoga" (*ādiyoga*) of the yoga of Śrī Vajrasattva; O sons of noble family, this has been explained.

Having cast the *phur pa* (ritual dagger), one should likewise request the departure from the secret maṇḍala itself by means of the hand as previously described. By reciting "JAḤ HŪṂ BAṂ HOḤ," one should visualize [the deities] entering into their own abodes in a particularly exalted manner. One should separate the colored powders with the syllable HŪṂ itself, collect them, and cast them into water. Regarding the command issued by the glorious Heruka for the sake of subduing wrathful beings with wrathful means: "That very one is the Blessed Yogin," and so forth—this refers to the "First Yoga of the Glorious Vajrasattva," which is proclaimed to noble sons.

Those who have desisted from the ten unwholesome actions, such as the taking of life, are said to possess purity of commitment (*samaya-viśuddhi*); their purification consists in their renunciation (*virati*). Having thus described the Blessed One—endowed with the sentiments (*rasa*) of the erotic and so forth, possessing eight faces, four feet, adorned with sixteen arms, and twenty-four eyes—the Blessed One is further described by this same method as having four faces and four arms, resplendent.

The purification of those who engage in the ten non-virtuous actions, such as taking life, and those whose commitments (*samaya*) have degenerated is now described; "purification" here means *viśuddhi*. Possessing the flavors [of conduct] such as "sporting" and so forth, with eight faces, four feet, and adorned with sixteen hands, the Blessed One has declared that he possesses twenty-four eyes. Furthermore, by that same sequence, the Blessed One has four faces and is fully embellished with four arms.

Therein, the first face is fierce; the second face on the right is terrifying with delusion; behind it is the third face, which has a wondrous mien of devouring; and to the left is the face of amorous kissing. Furthermore, the supreme *vaikaraṇa* is the upward-facing, distorted face. Emptiness (*śūnya*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) constitute the three faces of gnosis.
[Gloss added in the upper margin: "Emptiness" and so forth refer to the six faces of the six-armed deity.]

The first face is fierce; the second on the right is intoxicated with bliss and strikes with fear; the third face at the back is that of marvelous food; the face on the left is playful and laughs aloud. Likewise, the upper face called "the gaping one" is the supreme among all activities. The three faces are the wisdoms of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

He manifests the form of Akṣobhya, six-armed and likewise holding a vajra; yet, for those who fear prolixity, he further shows himself as two-armed and single-faced. On his left shoulder, in the manner of a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), he rests a *khaṭvāṅga* bearing a vajra and a bell. With his right hand, which holds a five-pronged blazing vajra with three-fold banners, he grasps a skull-cup filled with the Great Heart-mantra, forming the Great Mudrā. Seated in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*), he places his left foot upon the lap of the consort, while his right foot, in the manner of the "hero's seat" (*sattvaparyaṅka*), presses down upon her left thigh by joining the soles of the feet together.

The Vajra-holder with a form for the purpose of sporting (*mi bskyod pa'i gzugs can gyi rdo rje can*) likewise has six arms. To explain in detail: he is also taught as having one face and two arms; however, in his left armpit, by means of the application of pure offerings, he holds a *khaṭvāṅga* together with a vajra and a bell. His right hands hold a banner with three points, a *vajra-śakti*, and a blazing wheel. In his left hand, he fully grasps a skull-cup filled with great compassion. Regarding the so-called "eating" in the half-lotus posture of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*): sitting upon a high seat, he places his left foot on the ground and, through the application of the *sattvaparyaṅka* (heroic posture) with his right leg, he strikes. Furthermore, with the sole of that [right] foot, he presses down through the application of equalizing it with the left hip.

O Blessed One, this is the Raudrāsana posture. By means of this paryaṅka-mudrā, having caused the object of practice (*sādhya*) to fall, one should crush him by placing the left foot upon his head and encircling him with the right; then, having scattered [the remains] and visualized the form of the Wrathful One (*krodhamūrti*) facing upward above him, one should swallow the object of practice with that [form]. Having likewise meditated on the Blessed One facing upward above that very [object], one should take all women as desired through the yoga of the vajra-paryaṅka with the right foot, and effect union with them by the throbbing of the left thigh.

"O son of noble family, by means of this mudrā of the cross-legged posture while seated upon the fierce throne of the Blessed One, one will attain the accomplishment to be achieved. By churning with the left thigh and foot, one should visualize that wrathful body as being thoroughly expanded and pulverized; having meditated on it above the face of the Blessed One, one should drink that which is to be accomplished. One should likewise meditate on that very [body] above the face of the Blessed One. Then, by means of the right foot in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, one should take all women as one desires, and by moving the left thigh, one should engage in union with them."

Again, I shall describe the facial mudrās: in the eastern compartment, Gaurī has a gentle face; in the south, Caurī has a fierce face; behind [in the west], Pramohā has a face of blissful intoxication; on the left, Vetālī has a joyful face. In the southeast compartment, Pukkasī has a dancing face. In the southwest compartment, Caṇḍālī has a playful face through the yoga of seizing the life-force of others. In the northwest, Ghasmarī has a face that devours the dead through the yoga of chewing corpses. In the northeast, she resembles Heruka and possesses the form of the Blessed One; her gaze is peaceful. Gaurī has a fierce gaze, Caurī a bewildered gaze, Pramohā a gaze that revives the dead, Vetālī a dancing gaze, Pukkasī a downward gaze, Caṇḍālī an upward gaze, and Ghasmarā a devouring gaze.

Having visualized the flower as the form of Gaurī, whoever one gives it to becomes sealed. Incense is the form of Caurī; wine is the form of Pramohā; water is the form of Vetālī. The tree and creeper are Pukkasī; the bell is Caṇḍālī; fire is Ghasmarā. Through one-pointed union, one remains established in the yoga of meditative concentration.

Alternatively, one should proclaim the mudrās of their faces: in the eastern compartment is the white-faced Śāntī (Peaceful One); to the right is Caṇḍākṣī (Fierce-Eyed), who has the face of a thief; behind is Mūrcchanā (The Intoxicated), who has the face of Pramohā (The Deluded One) through the intoxication of bliss; to the left is Vetālī (Corpse-Woman). In the southeast is Pukkasī, who has the face of a dancer. In the southwest is Ḍombī, whose face is full of devotion toward all through her practice of snatching the life-force of others. In the northwest is Ghasmarī, who has the face of a corpse-eater. In the northeast is Herukākārā (She Who Has the Form of Heruka), who is the Blessed Lady. Śāntī has a peaceful gaze; Caṇḍākṣī has a fierce gaze; Pramohā has a deluded gaze; Vetālī has a gaze that summons the dead; Pukkasī has a dancing gaze; Ḍombī looks upward; Ghasmarī looks downward. Having visualized a flower as having the form of Śāntī, whichever [deity] it is offered to, that one will be sealed with the mudrā. For incense, it is the form of Caṇḍākṣī; for liquor, it is the form of Pramohā; for water, it is the form of Vetālī; for the wooden staff, it is Pukkasī; for the cloth, it is Caṇḍālī; for fire, it is Ghasmarī. One dwells in the application of meditative concentration through the single-pointed union.

Then, the connection should be made that Gaurī seals [the target] even through meditation (*dhyāna*). Likewise, through the yoga of the heart-abiding state, Caurī is the "heart-and-waist" [seal]. Having entered the body of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), one should contemplate the *sādhya* as being deluded by pleasure through the yoga of total infatuation (*pramoha*). Thus, Sukhapramadā causes infatuation. Through the meditation on Vettālī, one should sprinkle with the water of nectar; she raises the dead. Through the meditation on the sound of snapping fingers (*acchaṭānāda*), Pukkasī makes [the target] dance. Together with the meditation on the upward-moving breath (*ūrdhvaśvāsa*), Caṇḍālī causes [him] to move.
A very close parallel with the *Vajrajvālodayā*!

Furthermore, it should be joined with the statement: "One should also perform the mudrā-seal by means of that White Woman’s meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Thus, one should enter the body of the object of accomplishment through the meditative concentration drawn from the heart by the Female Thief (*caurī*), and draw [the essence] from the heart. Through the application of the Greatly Deluded One (*mūḍhā*), one should contemplate the object of accomplishment as being deluded and stupefied by bliss; thus, by bestowing supreme bliss, one causes great delusion. By the meditative concentration of the Vetālī, one revives the dead by sprinkling with the water of nectar (*amṛta*). By the yoga of the Pukkasī, one dances while brandishing a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*). By the meditative concentration of the Extremely Exhaling One (*ucchvāsā*) above, the Caṇḍālī brings about death through becoming unified as one.

*Ghasmarā* devours by means of eating (*aśana-bhakṣaṇa*), that is, through that meditation (*dhyāna*). She raises up *Gaurī*, who is the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*), by looking at her with a gaze fixed in meditation. Having entered the heart of the object of accomplishment with the mind, she draws it out by uprooting his heart-lotus with her left hand. *Caurī* kisses the face of the object of accomplishment with the mind. *Pramohā* deludes him directly or through the mind by means of the delusion of the face. *Vetālī* embraces and raises the dead; having unified herself with the object of accomplishment through the mind, she dances again. Through the yoga of *Pukkasī*, she causes him to dance; having become one with the object of accomplishment through the mind, she should cause an upward gaze by means of the delusion of the face. Through the yoga of *Caṇḍālī*, she kills. Through the yoga of *Ghasmarā*, having placed the object of accomplishment in her mouth, she should recite while chewing; the meaning is that all enemies become well-devoured.
% almost verbatim parallel with Vajrajvālodayā!

One should eat by means of the *ghasmarī* meditation, which consists of eating with food. With the gaze of the *kāminī*, one performs the mudrā by looking at the object of accomplishment from the left side. Having mentally entered the heart of the object of accomplishment, one draws it out and summons it by plucking the lotus of its heart with the left hand. The *caurī* draws [the essence] from the heart. The *mūrchinī* causes intense delusion through bliss, either mentally or directly. The *vetālī* brings about death by embracing the object of accomplishment mentally or directly. Through the yoga of the *pukkasī*, one performs the dance; having become one with the object of accomplishment mentally, one dances by oneself. Having become one with the object of accomplishment mentally, one performs the killing through the yoga of Caṇḍālī while maintaining the gaze above, intoxicated by bliss. Through the yoga of the *ghasmarī*, one places the object of accomplishment on a donkey and eats it. "To be eaten" means that all enemies will be utterly and perpetually consumed. This is the meaning.

He obtains the name Vajra-hūṃkāra, the Rescuer of the Three Worlds; that Vajrasattva shall become the Conqueror of the Three Worlds (*Trailokyavijaya*). Then, as for "another": from among Lalita, Karuṇābala, and so forth, one should choose another from the wrathful deities (*krodha*). Then, by means of wrath, [one asks]: "O Blessed One, what is the name of this one who utterly destroys wrath? For whose sake did he speak? They say it is for the sake of those who hold the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), grasping at a soul (*jīva*), a person (*pudgala*), and so on. This one is the ender of all conceptual constructions (*kalpa*); having conquered the wheel of the enemy of conceptualization (*kalpāri-cakra*) for them, he himself becomes the foremost siddhi of all conceptualizations. The Wrathful King named Vajrabhairava speaks: "Having reduced to ashes that which is terrifying, such as Haridvāra and the like—he is Vajrabhairava, the Great Passion (*mahārāga*). O Great Lover, the Vajra-Lover (*vajrarāga*) is the Vajrin (Vajradhara) who possesses that form. As it has been said: "Therefore, Vajrasattva, becoming reborn, shall become the Vajra-Lover. He has the luster of spring because he is adorned with fragrant flowers, pure clusters of blossoms, and so forth; and because he is endowed with the flower-bow of desire (*kāmoha-kusumacāpa*).

To the Vajra-hūṃ-kāra, the name "Deliverer of the Three Worlds" is attained; he is Vajrasattva, the one who is completely victorious over the three worlds. Then, the phrase "other than that" refers to the fixation upon all other wrathful deities—such as those of beauty, the power of compassion, and so forth—as having a single flavor within the wrathful state. "Bhagavān, what are the characteristics of the form of the Wrathful One? For what purpose was this spoken? Regarding the view of the body as a 'vessel,' the grasping at a self such as the life-force (*jīva*) and the person (*pudgala*), and the King of Death (*Yamarāja*), who brings an end to all permanence—it is the Lord of Siddhis, the supreme among all examinations, who is victorious over the wheel examined by those three. The "Wrathful King, Terrifier of Yama" shall now be explained. For this reason, starting from Viṣṇu and Maheśvara, all of them were reduced to dust by Vajrabhairava. Regarding the term "Great Passion" (*mahārāga*): "Great Passion" is Rāgavajra; it is described as being of his very nature. Furthermore, because he has become Vajrasattva and thus becomes the Rāgavajra, he is adorned with garlands of fragrant flowers like the *campaka*, with essences and so forth, and because he possesses the flower-bow and arrows, [the text says] "I am Desire."
