"Placed upon the vessel of the three bodies": one should visualize that the arrows placed upon the three planks in the middle of the *pṛṅkha*—beginning with the syllable *Oṃ*—are as if measured upon the head of the woman to be accomplished (*sādhya*). This is indicated by the end of the lotus for the sake of emission. Alternatively, it refers to the state of being melted by desire, like one who is melted by desire; "lotus" here means the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Thus, when she has been brought under control (*vaśyatā*) as if vomited forth, she emits [the essence] through such infinite supreme vows of all the Buddhas, beginning with these. Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vajra of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas.
The three beginning with the syllable *oṃ* should be observed;
for the purpose of protection from [the state of] flux.

And by means of [the syllables] beginning with *kṣarati* and so forth, the Tathāgata—the Vajra of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas—protects [them]. (Note: The manuscript A contains a lacuna for the portion corresponding to *sarvatathāgatākāyavākcittavajras tathāgataḥ*.)

Regarding the phrase "the arrangement of the three *s* of the arrow" (*sku gsum gyi mda’ ni rnam dgod pa*), it refers to the arrangement of the three syllables—*yūṃ*, *khāṃ*, and *āḥ*—in the center of the nock (*spang leb*) of the arrow. Together with the arrow, one should visualize these substances upon the crown of the consort’s head; it is said that they are placed at the edge of the lotus for the purpose of emission. If there is a request for desire, it is like making a request for desire. The so-called "lotus" (*padma*) is the heart (*snying po*); because it is brought under control like *e-vāṃ*, there is emission. "These and other such infinite supreme [teachings] are the supreme commitment (*samaya*) of all Buddhas"—thus spoke the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vajra Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas.

Then the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, said this to the Blessed One: "The arising of the [deities] has now been indicated; tell me now of the seats covered by the *viśvapaṭa* (all-pervading cloth), which are called *paṭṭas*. By means of these, the *avatārakas* (those who cause descent) and the *āvartāras* (those who cause turning back) [are established]; for that purpose, there is a yoga performed in the yoga of the descent of the *paṭa*. 'The arising of the [deities] has now been indicated' means that it is being brought to completion. [Bhagavān Vajrapāṇi] (variant: Vajrapāṇi).
Now his own rising has been indicated;
the seats covered with multicolored cloths have been prepared.
For that purpose;
in the yoga of the descent of the cloth;
by which.
[The word] *svodayam* is found in W; [the variant] *svādāyaḥ* is found in A.
[The phrase] *samprati sūcyate* is found in W; *saṃprasūcyate* is found in A.
[The gloss] *niṣpādyata ity arthaḥ* is found in W; *niṣpādya + + + +* is found in A.

Then the Blessed One and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi addressed the Blessed One in this way: “Please correctly proclaim your own arising, and now please explain it to me. Regarding the phrase “the covered painted images,” these refer to the seats; the entry into them is the yoga of their meaning, which is the yoga of entering the painted images. Therefore, one causes [them] to arise spontaneously. The phrase “correctly and thoroughly proclaimed” means “generated.”
That which is called the "lotus vessel" is known to be, in sequence, a human skull;
this is known to be a human skull.

Now I shall describe to you the arrangement of the inner apartments: the mandala of the Tathāgata is perfectly circular; that of Heruka is in the shape of a half-moon, meaning it has the color of wind—that is, the color blue. It is known to be in the form of a lotus and in the form of a jewel. "According to one's desire" means according to one's wish. Thus, in the center of the Tathāgata’s vajra, lotus, and jewel mandala-throne, whatever the practitioner desires, by removing the image of the Tathāgata and other [deities] and installing the image of Paramāśva instead, the mandala becomes that of Paramāśva and so forth.
The arrangement of the inner apartments;
the arrangement of the half-moon of Heruka;
according to one's desire.
The Tathāgata,
in the center of the mandala seat, according to one's desire;
the supreme horse and other mandalas.

Furthermore, I shall explain to you the configuration of the mandala of the consort: the palace of the Tathāgata is circular; the so-called "half-moon configuration of Heruka" means the configuration of the wind mandala. It should be understood as having the form of a lotus and the form of a jewel. "As desired" means according to one's inclination. Thus, in the center of the seats of the Tathāgata, Vajra, Padma, Ratna, and Khadga, whichever practitioner desires that very [deity] becomes the image of the Tathāgata and so forth. Subsequently, the image of the supreme horse should be placed; this is what is taught regarding the mandala of the supreme horse.

“According to what is available” means according to what has been obtained; that is, one should draw it with whatever collection of materials has come together for that particular mandala. “At the appropriate time”: one who desires pacification (śāntika) should draw it at dusk within the Tathāgata-maṇḍala; for the sake of enrichment (puṣṭi), as previously stated, one should draw it at midday or at midnight within the Ratna-maṇḍala; for the rite of sorcery (abhicārukarman), within the Vajra-maṇḍala; and for other rites, within the Padma-maṇḍala in the afternoon.

"According to how it was obtained" means "according to how it was acquired. One should draw [the mandala] using the very same implements that were produced for the purpose of the specific maṇḍala itself. Regarding "at whatever time": for one who desires pacification (*śānti*), that seat should be drawn in the center of a Tathāgata maṇḍala. For the sake of enrichment (*puṣṭi*), it should be drawn at sunrise within a Jewel (*ratna*) maṇḍala. For the rites of wrathful activity (*abhicāra*), it should be drawn at midday or midnight within a Vajra maṇḍala. For other rites, it should be drawn at sunset within a Lotus (*padma*) maṇḍala.

"At one's own pleasure" means that there is no restriction regarding the time for the *samaya* initiation. In the eight mandalas formed by the four lines drawn toward the east, west, north, and south, the *sampūrṇābhiṣeka* (complete initiation) is the *sarvācāryābhiṣeka* (initiation of a universal preceptor).

[The term *samayābhiṣeka* is found in manuscript A; it is also noted in W122 recto. [Regarding the phrase "in the eight mandalas formed by the four lines drawn toward the east, west, north, and south," this is the emendation; the variants in the manuscripts are as follows: W reads *prākpratīcyuttarāvākikcatuḥsūtrāṣṭamaṇḍale*, while A reads *prākpratītyucyantarāvāgdigdhātuḥ bhūtrāṣṭamaṇḍala*.]

The complete consecration [is] the consecration of all masters (*sarvācāryābhiṣeka*). Regarding [the phrase] "as one pleases" (*yathāsukha*), there is no fixed temporal restriction for the pledges (*samaya*) and the consecrations. By drawing four lines toward the eastern, southern, northern, and western directions, the maṇḍala becomes eightfold. The so-called "consecration of the full vessel" (*saṃpūrṇābhiṣeka*) refers to all the masters (*ācārya*).

All disciples are classified as superior, inferior, and middling. On the day of the inferior maṇḍala-consecration, [the mark] should be applied with sesame paste (*tilaka*). For the middling ones, it should be given with mother-of-pearl (*śuktikā*). As for those who are superior, [it is performed] by means of that which consists of a single Buddha. Regarding the phrase "a single-piece *ūrdhvaja*": *ekakhaṇḍika* and *mūrddhaja* together form *ekakhaṇḍikamūrddhaja*. A consecration should be performed by means of a single-piece [vessel], that is, one made from a single skull. An *ūrdhvaja* is a lotus-vessel. It is "single-piece" and has a single opening. It should be understood as being unbroken and without blemish. (Note: *madhyamāḥ* is corrected to *madhyamā* based on the manuscript evidence provided.)
The disciples [should be given] the initiation into the maṇḍala.
Of those who are supreme, their hair on the crown of the head (*mūrdhaja*)—and also the vajra upon the crown (*mūrdhavajra*).

One should understand that she should go [to him] while she is still intact and without wounds.

Regarding the phrase "the supreme disciple, the middle one, and the lowest one": for the lowest, the initiation of the mandala and the daytime *bindu* are given; for the middle, [the initiation] is performed with the *nyaphyi* (the cloth used for wiping). To those who are supreme, it should be bestowed by means of the single Buddha-nature alone. As for the term "one-headed" (*dum bu gcig pa'i mgo skyes*): "one-headed" refers to the single piece, and the "vajra of the head" is the "one-headed. The "one-headed" refers to the nature of the single-piece skull-cup (*kapāla*); the initiation should also be performed with this. "One-headed" means having a single opening; it should be understood as being uncracked and unbroken. "Head-born" (*mgo skyes*) refers to the lotus-vessel. "One-headed" means having a single aperture; it should be understood as being intact and undamaged.
It is called *kapāla* because it protects (*pālayati*) the head (*kaṃ*). As it has been said: "The perfected one consists of a single Buddha, and likewise consists of a single lotus."
Because it protects the aggregates of desire, it is a skull-cup. Likewise, it has been said: "The self-nature of all Buddhas is accomplished; I am likewise that single lotus."

The Vajra-jewel consecration of the Blessed One Vairocana; the Vajra consecration of Śrī Heruka; the Amitābha consecration and the central consecration should also be performed for those who recite [the mantras]. The Vajra consecration is half a jewel; the Jewel consecration is known as the Buddha-body. Akṣobhya is known as Vajrasattva by virtue of the nature of the fruit and cause of Paramāśva. The Vajra consecration.
In the center, the consecration of the half-vajra of jewels (ratnārdhavajrābhiṣeka) is to be performed; it is the Buddha-body (buddhakāya); [this is] the neck-consecration (manyābhiṣeka).
The supreme [nature] is Akṣobhya by virtue of his being the nature of both fruit and cause;
[this pertains to] Vajrasattva.

The empowerment of the precious Vajra of the Bhagavān Vairocana is the Vajra empowerment; the empowerment of Śrī Heruka is the Vajra empowerment; the empowerment of Amitābha is the Jewel empowerment, and it should also be applied there. The "half-jewel" is the Vajra empowerment; the body of all Buddhas should be known as the Jewel empowerment. It is also that of the Supreme Steed (Ucchuṣma). By virtue of its nature as cause and fruit, it is also to be known as Vajrasattva, the Unshakeable.

What is this *kapālāsana*, wherein [the goal] is to be accomplished? It is beneficial by its very nature and established through its own power (*prabhāva*). "Power" means capacity, which consists in the state of being devoid of the conceptual construction of subject and object. By that very power as it truly is, it is established by nature. By that very reality, what is to be accomplished through the exertion of this *thod pa'i gdan* (the skull-throne)? It is established by its own nature (*svabhāva*), because the power arising from that very nature emerges as its accomplishment; since it is of a nature that leaves no room for the conceptualization of subject and object through the capacity emerging from that nature, it is established by the emergence of that very state, being perfected by its own essence.

"The form of the crown of skulls and garlands is the *svabhāvaka* (nature-arisen) [state]" means: because of non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). This is what is being said: just as the heat of fire is established by its very nature, so too, by its very power, there is the natural purity (*prakṛtiviśuddhi*) of that [gnosis]. Having performed the yoga of the true reality and the commitment (*samaya*), there is a state of oneness with all gnosis. Such a yoga is to be understood as belonging to all the Tathāgatas and others. "The *svabhāvaka* [state]" is because of non-dual gnosis. Just as [the heat] of fire...
In the same way, even for that [being],

The phrase "from the nature of the form of the Ornament of the Garland of Thod-pa" means that it was spoken thus from non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). For example, fire is established as having the nature of heat; likewise, because its very manifestation is naturally pure, if one performs the yoga of the virtuous intention of that [nature], through the yoga of becoming one with the Wisdom Being (*jñānasattva*) in a state of identity, one should realize all the Tathāgatas.

Having mentally inscribed the syllable *HŪṂ* upon the moon at one’s own heart and uttering that very same [syllable], one should contemplate oneself as being equal to space. By means of that very [syllable], one should again visualize a lunar disc in the form of a lunar disc, and above that, a five-pronged vajra through the cultivation of the pride of Vajrasattva. Then, having brought about the entry of all the Tathāgatas into that [vajra] and having manifested Vajrasattva, one should descend and manifest him seated upon a lotus throne; and according to one’s capacity, one should establish Locanā and the others in emanation—this is the meaning.

Having visualized the syllable *Hūṃ* within the moon at one’s own heart and recited it, one should contemplate oneself as being equal to space. That very moon-maṇḍala is itself a moon-maṇḍala. Upon that, one should also meditate on a five-pronged vajra with the syllable *Hūṃ*. Therein, all the Tathāgatas are inserted; having generated Vajrasattva there as well, he is summoned and requested to sit upon the lotus seat. This is the meaning of the statement that he should also abide as the emanations of Locanā and the others.

In this same way, the arising of one's own family for Vairocana and the others should also be understood through the application [of the method]. And by this very application, their arising is comparable to the moon, the sun, and so forth. By removing both external and internal darkness, the arising and production of all the deities is accomplished. This is the procedure for the arising of the expansion of all activities.

In this way, one should observe the application of the elements belonging to the respective families of Vairocana and the others. By means of this application, whatever arises from them is like the emergence of the sun and moon. Because they arise as the five syllables from both the external and internal natures, all goddesses are born from the two and are perfected. This is the ritual for the extensive manifestation of all activities.

"In some places" means unspecified. From the penetration of one's own mind comes the *bodhicitta*. One who attains enlightenment for the sake of all beings is a *bodhisattva*; his conduct is *bodhicaryā*. Because he follows [beings] without failing to reach them according to their capacity, he is "the follower" (*anuga*). He abides in the form of the triad of brothers: Jayakara, Madhukara, and Sarvārthasādhaka. Through this form, there is the welfare of sentient beings. His various manifestations are his "births" (*jāti*). Since he arises from the essence of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, he is pure; therefore, he is Samantabhadra. Thus, the noble *bodhicaryā* is "according to the follower. As before.

"La la" means "not seeing. Because it is the individual discernment of one's own mind, it is the *bodhicitta* (awakened mind). A bodhisattva is a hero who has cast [himself] toward awakening; his conduct is the "conduct of awakening," which follows in accordance with having correctly attained the state of a hero. By way of abiding in the forms of the three lords—the Victor (*Jaya*), the Honey-Producer (*Madhukara*), and the Accomplisher of All Aims (*Sarvārthasādhaka*)—he acts for the benefit of sentient beings. He manifests in various transformations, such that even dust, darkness, and the strength of the heart become for the sake of sentient beings. That which is completely pure is Samantabhadra. Therefore, this "conduct of awakening" is called "following in accordance" just as described above.

The mass of merit that clearly brings about the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary characteristics—of that mass, the dust particles are the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and their buds are the eighty secondary characteristics. What is that [mass]? It is the collection and transformation of those qualities and so forth, which are the teachers of clarity; it is the great journey toward enlightenment.

Regarding the phrase "arising clearly from space": for the sake of sentient beings, the thirty-two marks of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*) and the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*) are perfected. The dust motes of that mass of merit are the thirty-two marks of a Great Being; the dust motes of those [marks] are the minor marks. What is this "clarity"? Clarity refers to the apprehension of qualities and so forth in their excellence; the offering to Great Enlightenment is that which is completely surrounded by the accumulation of these.

Because he does not harm the Bodhisattvas even in the form of Māra, or because he slays the minds of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, he is Māra; [yet] as Vajrarāga, he is the conqueror of Māra through the destruction of the four Māras. Śākyamuni, having become fully awakened, is the one who effects liberation through purity by rejecting the grasping at phenomena (*dharma*) and persons (*pudgala*). For the sake of worldly yogins, there is the rejection of the person; for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, there is the rejection of the grasping at phenomena. Thus, the realization of the selflessness of persons and phenomena results in the complete purity of liberation through knowing things as they truly are. For this purpose, the Blessed One Vairocana is the turner of the Wheel of Dharma.
The realization of the selflessness of persons and phenomena;
as it truly is.

The Bodhisattva being deceived by the form of a Māra is the Māra of birth; because he slays the minds of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, Māra is the vajra of desire. Having conquered the four Māras and triumphed over them, in one instance Śākyamuni became the Fully Enlightened One (*abhisambuddha*). Because he has severed the grasping at phenomena (*dharma*) and persons (*pudgala*), there is the purity of liberation. Because he has severed the grasping at persons who are worldly yogins, and because he has severed the grasping at the dharmas of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, he thus realizes the selflessness of phenomena and persons. Through the thorough knowledge of things as they are, all liberations are pure; for this purpose, the Blessed One Vairocana turns the wheel of Dharma.

Its purification consists of sixty-two aspects; in reality, it is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) due to the non-apprehension of a self. For that purpose, Avalokiteśvara becomes King Padmanarteśvara.
The absence of intrinsic nature [is established] through non-apprehension;
for that purpose.

The sixty-two types of views of self (*ātman*), all forms of attachment, and their purification—since the self is not observed within suchness and is thus devoid of intrinsic nature—the Lord of the Sovereigns of the Lotus Dance is, for that purpose, the Sovereign King of Avalokiteśvara.

From the Tuṣita gods, all around, [arises] the supreme wheel; the supreme wheel of the deities of the mantra, which is the cause of various miraculous powers (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*). Furthermore, O sons of good family, it is said: "by the assembly of all Buddhas. An assembly (*samāja*) is a gathering. "Sukhāvatī, the supreme mind, Tuṣita"—O sons of good family, [this place] is like the world-system Sukhāvatī. Just as the world-system Sukhāvatī is adorned by the assembly of all Tathāgatas, so too the Blessed One, Śrī Padmanarteśvara, is surrounded on all sides by immeasurable Tathāgatas such as Śrī Vairocana; therefore, he is like the world-system Sukhāvatī. For that reason, there shall be the arising of the savior Padmanarteśvarī.
To the gods;

"The excellent wheel is the ultimate of all the gods of Tuṣita. The supreme among various miraculous displays is the excellent wheel of the gods. For instance, noble son, regarding the term 'assembly of all Buddhas,' 'assembly' means a gathering. 'Sukhāvatī' means the supreme Tuṣita; noble son, it is like the world-system of Sukhāvatī. For example, just as the world-system of Sukhāvatī is adorned by the assembly of all Tathāgatas, likewise, because it is completely surrounded by immeasurable Tathāgatas such as the Blessed One Padmanarteśvara and Śrī Vairocana, it is like the world-system of Sukhāvatī; for that purpose, the savior Padmanarteśvara appears."

The Sun-like Great Seal (Sūryamahāmudrā) is so called because it is like the sun; it is the Great Seal that, through the gift consisting in the non-apprehension of the giver, the recipient, and the act of giving, effects the abandonment of stinginess, which is ultimate purity. It is for that purpose, and in order to engage all beings in absolute giving by means of the knowledge of the complete purity of the three spheres, that it is the Sun-like Great Seal. Regarding "Ākāśagarbha": space (*ākāśa*) is the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*), and he whose "womb" (*garbha*)—that is, his cause of origination—is this [gnosis], is thus designated.

The meaning is as follows: because generosity that does not perceive a gift, a giver, or a recipient abandons avarice, for the sake of that ultimate purity, sentient beings who are avaricious are applied to supreme giving through the primordial wisdom of the complete purity of the three spheres. "The Sun-like Mahāmudrā" refers to the Seal of the Sun. Regarding "the Essence of Space," it is so called because the essence is generated from the primordial wisdom of equality within space; he spoke thus because it is exactly so.

Because she possesses mastery over all supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), she is the fulfiller of all hopes. The "hopes" (*āśā*) of all sentient beings consist of their various prayers for states such as that of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); by granting these, she is the fulfiller of all hopes. Therefore it is said: "From space, she brings forth all excellent jewels, such as women and so forth; she is the one who sets in motion all jewels. She is the one who sets in motion the seven jewels. For this purpose, Tārā becomes the Conqueror of the Three Worlds (*Trailokyavijayā*).

The Sovereign of All Siddhis who Completely Fulfills All Intentions is she who fulfills the intentions of all sentient beings by granting their wishes through the prayers they offer for universal sovereignty (*cakravartitva*) and so forth in every possible way. Therefore, it was said: "In the sky, she causes a rain of all the seven precious jewels, such as elephants and the rest"—meaning she causes a rain of the seven treasures. For that purpose, the emergence of Tārā is her victory over the three worlds.

Purification occurs through haṭhayoga.

With his first left foot, he tramples upon the three-eyed Viṣṇu; with the second [left foot], he stands trampling upon the third, Brahmā, and Kāmadeva. By this, it is shown that he possesses eight arms.

The Lord of All Siddhis, on his supreme steed, gathered the three worlds—the Great Deity and the rest—and subdued them through taking refuge in the Three Jewels and other means. Then, having crushed all three worlds with the Vajra-Hūṃkara, the Great Deity offered the *Pratyaṅgirā* (the Reversal of Difficulties) to the Guru as a gift and was raised up. This is the meaning of the phrase "completely filled with the graceful goddesses and so forth," which refers to the drawing of the lines for the mandala in its proper sequence, consisting of four corners, four gates, and the intermediate spaces.

By what measurement of the mandala should one mark out the lines? The intention is as follows: one cubit for the interior, one cubit for the middle, and likewise one cubit for the exterior; thus, the three-fold enclosure (tripuṭa) shall be two cubits [in total].
Regarding the question of by what measurement the maṇḍala lines should be drawn:

"one cubit within" means one cubit in the center; this intends that there should be one cubit on the outside and two cubits for the third [outer] row. "Resembling the moon’s orb" means, as the Blessed One has said, that the inner maṇḍala should be circular. This is the maṇḍala that uplifts the three worlds.

Regarding the phrase "like the lunar mandala," the Blessed One, the Savior of the Three Worlds, taught that the essence of the mandala is circular; thus he spoke of the Mandala of the Savior of the Three Worlds.

The cultivation of the remedies (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*), which is the cultivation of the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣyabhāvanā*), must now be explained. Among these, first of all, [the cultivation of the remedies]: *pratipakṣabhāvanā* (cultivation of the remedy) is the correct reading, whereas *pratipakṣasya bhāvanā* (cultivation of the remedy) is an alternative; likewise, *˚pakṣya˚* (conducive to awakening) is the corrected term, while *˚pakṣa˚* (wing/side) and *˚pakṣyā˚* (feminine form) are variants found in the manuscripts.

For it is through the body that corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*) is manifested; by examining that, one enters into the truth of suffering.

Now, the meditation on the discordant factors and the meditation on the factors conducive to awakening shall be explained. In that regard, first of all, improper mental engagement (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) is the cause of craving. Because one enters into the Four Truths through the absence of delusion, the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) constitutes the proper meditation upon the body; by thoroughly investigating that [body], one enters into the Truth of Suffering.

Regarding the phrase "because the lineage (*gotra*) is also completely pure": "lineage" refers to the nature (*svabhāva*), that is, the essential identity. Regarding the phrase "in order to attain the marks and signs": it is for the sake of attaining the major marks and minor signs of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*), and for the sake of purifying the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*); thus, Bodhisattvas engage in them. Furthermore, in order to train in the powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth, one should understand that the fourteen kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) are established here. Moreover, what is emptiness in this context?
The non-existence of the person (*pudgala*) and of phenomena (*dharma*) is emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
the actual existence of that non-existence therein is another emptiness. (1.20) [The word *abhāvaḥ* is supplied.]
Emptiness;
[the existence of] reality.

The non-existence of the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*), and the existence of that very non-existence, is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Regarding that aforementioned [subject], such as the enjoyer and so forth, there is this "other" emptiness. For the purpose of explaining the characteristic of emptiness, he establishes emptiness in two ways at the conclusion: the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*). These are respectively for the purpose of avoiding the superimposition (*samāropa*) of a person and phenomena, and the denial (*apavāda*) of their emptiness. In this way, the classification of emptiness is to be understood. How is its proof to be understood?

The non-substantiality of phenomena (*dharma*) and persons (*pudgala*), which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), is such that the ultimate reality arising from it is empty of itself therein, and is the singular reality arising from the non-substantiality of external phenomena and persons. Regarding this, because of the profundity and so forth as previously described, the sixteen types of emptiness should be established in two systems for the purpose of explaining their characteristics. That is, the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*). One should understand the distinctions of emptiness according to their respective order, for the purpose of completely abandoning all forms of emptiness that correctly apply to phenomena and persons. How should one understand how they are established?
If this [nature] were not defiled, all embodied beings would be liberated.
If this [defilement] were not pure, then effort would be fruitless. (1.21)

If this were not afflicted from the very beginning, all embodied beings would be liberated. If this were not pure, effort would be fruitless. If the emptiness of phenomena were not afflicted by adventitious secondary afflictions even when the antidote has not arisen, then, due to the absence of affliction, all sentient beings would be liberated without any exertion.
Since the emptiness of phenomena is such that adventitious afflictions have not arisen, it is not defiled by the discordant factors; yet, because affliction would be non-existent,
all sentient beings would be liberated without any effort at all.

Furthermore, even if the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) has arisen, [the mind] would not become purified; thus, the undertaking for the sake of liberation would be fruitless. And having established this, [it follows that] the undertaking for the sake of liberation [would be pointless].
And thus,

if it were not purified by the removal of its discordant factors (*vipakṣa*), even that which is unarisen would not be purified, and the exertion for the sake of liberation would be fruitless. If this were the case, it would be neither afflicted (*kliṣṭā*) nor non-afflicted, neither pure (*śuddhā*) nor impure (*aśuddhā*).
Nor is it undefiled; nor indeed is it undefiled.
How so? Because it is by its very nature neither undefiled nor impure.
It is neither afflicted nor impure,
because the mind is luminous by its very nature.
How is it neither afflicted nor [even] impure?
It is neither afflicted nor non-afflicted; it is neither pure nor [impure].
Because affliction is adventitious. [1.22]

Because the nature of the mind is luminosity, it is neither afflicted nor non-afflicted, neither pure nor impure. How so? It is not afflicted, nor is it impure, because the mind is luminous by nature; yet it is not unafflicted, nor is it pure, because afflictions are adventitious.

"From the distinction of the stages (*bhūmi*), the distinction of qualities will arise. For example, if an elephant eats a *ketaka* flower, it turns into substances such as musk; if an ordinary elephant eats it, it turns into dung. Likewise, even desire and the like, when abiding in the stages of purification, will ripen into the fruit of excellence through the application of the distinction of intention."

Just as milk, when consumed by snakes and the like, transforms into the nature of poison, whereas when consumed by other persons, it attains the state of nectar; so too, those sons of good family, because they arise from a particular disposition (*āśaya*), bring about distinguished results, since their nature is inherently faultless.
